#9097. The astonishing, untold story of Marie-Anne “Baby” de Goldschmidt-Rothschild, who smuggled a Van Gogh painting and the artist's letters out of Nazi Europe

Marie-Anne “Baby” de Goldschmidt-Rothschild (1920s)

Photograph by Ernst Schneider, Laure de Margerie collection

Adventures with Van Gogh is a weekly blog by Martin Bailey, The Art Newspaper's long-standing correspondent and expert on the Dutch painter. Published on Fridays, stories range from newsy items about this most intriguing artist, to scholarly pieces based on meticulous investigations and discoveries.

Explore all of Martin’s adventures with Van Gogh here.

Among the early Van Gogh collectors was a young woman who had just turned 22. Born in 1892 to a very wealthy German family, Marie-Anne (nicknamed “Baby”) de Goldschmidt-Rothschild certainly had the money, but also avant-garde taste. She bought one of the artist’s finest portraits.

Her amazing story is told in a meticulously researched new book: A Collector’s Odyssey: How Marie-Anne de Goldschmidt-Rothschild saved her Paintings from Nazi Looting, written by Christel Force, Anna-Carolin Augustin and Katharina Weiler and published in Berlin by De Gruyter (it is freely downloadable).

Van Gogh’s The Arlésienne (November 1888)

Musée d’Orsay, Paris (Donation sous réserve d'usufruit Mme R. de Goldschmidt-Rothschild, 1952 © photo : RMN-Grand Palais (Musée d’Orsay) / Stéphane Maréchalle)

It may come as a surprise that the very first painting bought by Marie-Anne (whose maiden name was Friedländer-Fuld) was a Van Gogh - and an important one. Encouraged by progressive mentors, in June 1914 she purchased The Arlésienne (November 1888), a portrait of the artist’s friend Marie Ginoux, co-owner of the Café de la Gare in Arles. The picture cost the equivalent of £6250, a very large sum for a Van Gogh at the time. (There is another version at New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art)

Marie-Anne later recounted how she hung the portrait, on antique-gold wallpaper, in her suite in the family’s palatial residence in Berlin’s Pariser Platz, almost next to the Brandenburg Gate: “My first and only painting, at the centre [of her main room], dominating everything and everyone, was L’Arlésienne by Van Gogh”. Her father, who had much more traditional tastes, abhorred the artist, telling her to hide “the jaundiced old lady” behind a curtain.

Marie-Anne de Goldschmidt-Rothschild, with her Louis XV sofa and Van Gogh’s The Arlésienne in her Berlin mansion (1929)

Photograph by Ernst Schneider, De Querschnitt journal (Berlin), September 1929

This was only the beginning. Marie-Anne went on to collect other Impressionist artists and their followers: Paul Gauguin, Claude Monet, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Edouard Manet, Paul Cezanne and Pablo Picasso.

By the time Marie-Anne was 31, she had married three times: to the English aristocrat John Mitford, the former German foreign minister Richard von Kühlmann and the aristocratic banker Rudolf von Goldschmidt-Rothschild (he used “von”, while she preferred “de”). After a few years, she and Rudolf lived independently and eventually divorced in 1938.

With the rise of the Nazis, Marie-Anne, who was of Jewish heritage, smuggled the Van Gogh portrait twice. The first time was in 1934, a year after Hitler came to power, when she secretly sent the painting from Berlin to her residence in Paris. This required subterfuge: she commissioned an artist friend, Eugen Spiro, to paint identical copies of her most important paintings. The copy of The Arlésienne was then surreptitiously placed in the frame in her Berlin mansion, with no one apparently noticing the switch.

The Van Gogh and the other canvasses were taken off their stretchers and rolled up. Marie-Anne instructed Marie-Anne instructed her (female) servants to each carry a single roll to Paris, without telling them what was inside. Had the pictures been declared at the border, Nazi officials would have prevented them from being exported or would have charged her an exorbitant tax. The Arlésienne safely arrived at Marie-Anne's mansion in Paris on the Rue de la Faisanderie.

Six years later, France was threatened by Germany. In mid-May 1940, a month before the Nazi occupation of Paris, Marie-Anne decided to flee to the US, protecting her life and collection. By that time, the only route was via Portugal, which was neutral. In a move which the book’s co-author Force describes as “reckless and admirable in equal measure”, Marie-Anne hatched a plan for her most important paintings.

She took the canvases strapped to the roof of her Citroën. Amidst the chaos of millions fleeing Paris, she drove across France to Spain, facing seemingly endless logistical challenges, but eventually reaching Portugal. Although some reports suggest the Van Gogh was transported on the roof with the rest of the paintings, Marie-Anne later told a different story.

According to her, The Arlésienne had been sent earlier to Amsterdam, on loan for an exhibition. Just one week before the German invasion in May 1940, her contact in the Netherlands somehow managed to get the Van Gogh onto an aircraft bound for Lisbon.

In her hotel room in Portugal, Marie-Anne rolled up all her paintings, although the thick impasto paint of The Arlésienne created problems. She then covered the whole roll with a protective tarpaulin. Eventually she secured a place on a liner crossing the Atlantic, bound for Mexico.

After her ship finally arrived at Veracruz, Marie-Anne travelled on to Mexico City, later taking a plane to Texas and another flight on to New York, accompanied by her paintings. The Arlésienne had been travelling during wartime for nearly five months, arriving in New York in November 1940.

Marie-Anne, thanks to her immense wealth and elite contacts, had managed to escape the terrible fate of the vast majority of continental European Jewry.

In 1928, Marie-Anne made another prescient purchase: a collection of 22 letters written by Van Gogh in 1887-89 to his artist friend Emile Bernard (plus one to Gauguin). The bulk of Vincent’s surviving letters remained with Theo and his heirs, so the Bernard correspondence represented a very important acquisition. Many of the letters also included small sketches of the paintings which Van Gogh was working on.

Van Gogh’s letter to Emile Bernard, around 19 June 1888 (extracts)

Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation)

When the art lover and writer Harry Kessler visited Marie-Anne in 1929, he noted in his diary that they had dined under The Arlésienne. Kessler then recorded: “After dinner, thirty letters by Van Gogh in an excessively ornate, ugly binding, were passed around with cigarettes and coffee.” (Although Kessler said it was 30 letters, it was actually 23.) Contrasting the opulence with the artist’s simple way of life, Kessler added: “Poor Van Gogh!”

In 1940, when Marie-Anne fled from Paris in her Citroën, she carried this ornately-bound volume of Van Gogh’s correspondence in a suitcase. She kept the letters during her American wartime exile.

On 26 August 1944, just hours after Paris was liberated, Marie-Anne wrote from California to the Free France delegation in Washington, DC: “My hand is shaking with emotion as I am writing to you today, day of the Liberation of Paris. I turn to you to ask that whoever is concerned be informed that I bequeath my Van Gogh painting L’Arlésienne to the city of Paris. It is at the Louvre, I expect, that it will find its place.”

Marie-Anne left New York and returned to Europe in 1947, once again taking her paintings with her. Her family’s palatial residence in Berlin had been almost totally destroyed by Allied bombs, and she wanted to settle in her mansion in Paris. There she would spend the rest of her life, until her death in 1973.

The dining room in Marie-Anne de Goldschmidt-Rothschild’s Paris mansion (1950s)

Photograph by Antoinette Georges Perrier, De Goldschmidt-Rothschild family archive

Marie-Anne had lived with The Arlésienne for nearly 60 years. After her death, the painting went to the Louvre, which displayed it in the Jeu de Paume. It was transferred to the Musée d’Orsay when it opened in 1986.

We can report that next year The Arlésienne will be presented in an exhibition at the Musée de l’Orangerie in Paris: Dépossédes: Oeuvres spoliées, vies brisées 1933-45 (Dispossessed: Plundered Art, Shattered Lives 1933–45)(October 2027-January 2028). Marie-Anne’s life certainly had its challenges, but it was hardly shattered like most of the other collectors who will be featured in the show.

As for the Van Gogh correspondence, Marie-Anne donated one letter to the Fondation Custodia in Paris, another somehow left her collection and the one addressed to Gauguin was given to a friend. This left 20 letters which she bequeathed to her grandson, Frédéric de Goldschmidt-Rothschild. He sold the group to the New York dealer and collector Eugene Thaw in 2001.

Thaw later recalled how he bought the letters: “A young man [the grandson] showed up in my office with them all under his arm—unframed, unmatted—in a simple folder. And of course I nearly died of pleasant shock at seeing them.” Marie-Anne’s ornate binding had already gone.

The correspondence was generously donated by Thaw to New York’s Morgan Library & Museum. These important Van Gogh letters, with their 14 sketches, are now reunited online with the rest of the artist’s correspondence.

For conservation reasons, Van Gogh's letters to Bernard are very rarely exhibited, but I once had the privilege of examining the originals in the Morgan’s study room. Seeing the letters, penned by the artist on ordinary writing paper with his little sketches, I thought back to when they had once been housed in Marie-Anne’s ornate album—and their perilous journey during the war.

Martin Bailey is a leading Van Gogh specialist and special correspondent for The Art Newspaper. He has curated exhibitions at the Barbican Art Gallery, Compton Verney/National Gallery of Scotland and Tate Britain.

Martin has written a number of bestselling books on Van Gogh’s years in France: The Sunflowers Are Mine: The Story of Van Gogh's Masterpiece (Frances Lincoln 2013, UK and US), Studio of the South: Van Gogh in Provence (Frances Lincoln 2016, UK and US), Starry Night: Van Gogh at the Asylum (White Lion Publishing 2018, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale: Auvers and the Artist’s Rise to Fame (Frances Lincoln 2021, UK and US). The Sunflowers are Mine (2024, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale (2024, UK and US) are also now available in a more compact paperback format.

His other recent books include Living with Vincent van Gogh: The Homes & Landscapes that shaped the Artist (White Lion Publishing 2019, UK and US), which provides an overview of the artist’s life. The Illustrated Provence Letters of Van Gogh has been reissued (Batsford 2021, UK and US). My Friend Van Gogh/Emile Bernard provides the first English translation of Bernard’s writings on Van Gogh (David Zwirner Books 2023, UKand US).

To contact Martin Bailey, please email vangogh@theartnewspaper.com

#9096. Hollywood and Analog Photography Power Kodak’s Fifth Consecutive Quarter of Growth

Hollywood and Analog Photography Power Kodak’s Fifth Consecutive Quarter of Growth

It has now been five straight quarters of growth for the transformed, resurgent Eastman Kodak.

After facing immense financial challenges for decades, including warnings about its ability to continue as a “going concern” last year, Eastman Kodak has risen from the ashes like a phoenix, cashing in on analog’s revival.

The star of the show for the Rochester, New York-based Kodak is its Advanced Materials and Chemicals (AM&C) division, which posted 21% revenue growth in Q3 2026 compared to Q3 2025. While AM&C’s $99 million in revenue is significantly less than Kodak’s $165 million in Print revenue, the Print division’s revenue actually dipped 7% year-over-year. In total, Kodak’s consolidated revenues of $276 million this past quarter are up 3%. Profits are up, too, increasing by 7%.

“Kodak delivered strong performance in the third quarter, once again achieving year-over-year improvement in revenue, gross profit and Operational EBITDA,” says Jim Continenza, Kodak’s Executive Chairman and CEO, in SEC filings.

“We continue to execute our long-term plan and are seeing a return on our ongoing investments. Our primary growth engine, AM&C, is now our fastest-growing, most profitable unit. Our print business has performed well for the year to date despite challenging economic conditions. And, most importantly, we generated $27 million in cash for Q3, an important indicator of the operational strength of our business. Looking forward, we’re focused on continuing to invest in our core businesses and finishing the year with profitable growth,” Continenza continues.

As Continenza says, AM&C is Eastman Kodak’s fastest-growing and most profitable business unit. What exactly is AM&C, though? Kodak says AM&C covers the manufacturing of still, motion picture, and industrial films, plus specialty chemicals related to film, technologies, and medicine.

As CineD reports, in a call with investors, Continenza specifically called out the growing desire among Hollywood filmmakers to shoot their biggest projects on film.

“Film continues to be the capture medium of choice for major features,” Continenza told investors.

While Christopher Nolan’s record-breaking IMAX epic, The Odyssey, made a lot of headlines for its use of over two million feet of film, it is just one example of the return of film to Hollywood. Kodak had a great story about The Odyssey in August that dug a bit deeper into the movie’s use of Kodak film.

Kodak says award-winning cinematographer and Director of Photography Hoyte van Hoytema used Kodak Vision3 250D 5207 for daytime exteriors and bright interiors, and Kodak Vision3 500T 5219 for low-light and night scenes.

“The 250D and 500T are my sweet spot filmstocks. I love their grain structures and they’re very much my functional workhorses. The way I work with lenses, NDs, daylight and lights for night scenes, falls within the sensitivity curves of both those stocks. They are both versatile too. For example, I can shoot a little bit longer into magic hour with the 250D and I don’t have to resort too quickly into going higher-up in ASA,” van Hoytema told Kodak.

Earlier this year, Kodak celebrated seven movies shot on Kodak that competed for the Palme d’Or at Cannes 2026, and the legendary film company routinely updates its list of productions shot on film.

Paper Tiger, Disclosure Day, and Marty Supreme are just a few big names on the list. Continenza also mentioned Sense and Sensibility and Digger in his call.

Then, of course, there’s Eastman Kodak’s growing still film business. Over the past year-plus, Eastman Kodak has brought photographic film sales back under its purview, rebranding many different stocks and even unveiling some new, albeit familiar, ones. The company reintroduced some larger-format photo film stocks a few months ago, too.

Between Hollywood’s reignited love affair with film and Eastman Kodak’s investment in both motion picture and still film production, it’s immediately evident that Eastman Kodak believes its path to future success goes through analog. The licensing deals for smash hit Kodak-branded products don’t hurt, either.

#9095. Meet AMAA, Neri&Hu’s pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

Photography by Mikael Olsson unless stated

An innovative approach to the reuse of existing buildings defines the output of Italian architecture office AMAA, which Neri&Hu has selected as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design as part of Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler.

Led by Marcello Galiotto and Alessandra Rampazzo, over the past 14 years AMAA has become known for its approach to the reuse of post-industrial structures in northern Italy, with the transformation of a former factory building into its own studio, a typical example of its approach.

According to Galiotto, these buildings are a taste of what the studio wants to achieve.

“What we have done in the past 10 years is really just a sketch of what we can do in the future,” he told Dezeen.

“Our research is still growing, and it can be applied to various programmes and contexts,” he continued, “but in 20 years we will both be 60 so we want the studio to be able to evolve and grow in new directions.”

The preservation and adaptation of existing buildings, which is central to AMAA’s practice, is a key reason why architects Lyndon Neri and Rossana Hu selected the studio for Dezeen’s 20×20 series.

“AMAA is significant for its fierce commitment to adaptive reuse,” said the duo, adding that the studio’s ability to repurpose historic structures “positions them as leaders in circular, life-cycle thinking in contemporary Italian architecture”.

AMAA is significant for its fierce commitment to adaptive reuse, [which] positions them as leaders in circular, life-cycle thinking in contemporary Italian architecture

Galiotto and Rampazzo met Neri and Hu when they participated in the 2023 Venice Biennale and have since been invited to host lectures at the University of Pennsylvania, where Hu is chair of the architecture department.

“We have a long relationship with Lyndon and Rossana who we consider to be both amazing people and great architects so it’s truly an honour to be selected by them,” said Galiotto.

Rampazzo added that she saw a clear overlap between Shanghai-based Neri&Hu’s work, which also has a focus on adaptive reuse approach, and their approach at AMAA.

“I’m a fan of their work and I see similarities in the way we do architecture and also the way we teach, despite our different cultural backgrounds,” she said. “I also love how they really support students and young architects by sharing their knowledge. We have a lot to learn from them but I hope we can have the same kind of legacy.”

Rampazzo and Galiotto have known each other for more than 20 years after meeting while studying architecture at the Iuav University of Venice.

The studio now has offices in Venice and in the industrial town of Arzignano, and has gradually become established among Italy’s most respected architecture firms thanks to projects such as their own office and a cafe housed within a 19th-century town hall.

We felt our education hadn’t provide us with knowledge of how to run a medium or large-scale practice, so my experience with Sou Fujimoto was about closing the gap between the present and future of our studio

The pair studied together at Iuav under the professorship of Massimo Carmassi, who they cite as an important influence on their approach to restoration and reuse.

After graduating in 2010, they assisted Carmassi and briefly set up a studio with friends to work on competitions. Then Galiotto went to Japan to work for Sou Fujimoto, while Rampazzo travelled to India for her PhD studies.

“We felt our education hadn’t provide us with knowledge of how to run a medium or large-scale practice,” said Galiotto, “so my experience with Sou Fujimoto was about closing the gap between the present and future of our studio.”

This global travel and work experience helped open their minds to alternative approaches and opportunities, as well as giving them the confidence to set up their own studio back in Venice.

“We’re still evolving, and evolving our identity,” said Galiotto. “But the important thing was to find ourselves. That’s why the path was complicated.

“Stay in Italy… going outside of Italy… travelling the world as much as we can to see things. That was the key, I think, to the position that we are covering right now in the panorama of architecture in Italy.”

In 2015, they opened a branch office in Galiotto’s hometown of Arzignano, which has been described as an “AMAA playground” due to the number of projects the practice has completed there.

Galiotto pointed out that their work in the town is part of an ongoing research into how architecture can blur the line between private and public spaces, with the Caffe Nazionale project providing a good example.

“Although the cafe is privately owned, it also forms the edge of a plaza so we wanted to give the space back to the people,” the architect explained, adding that the studio has coined the term “super public” to describe this aspect of their practice.

Alongside their work in Arzignano and Venice, AMAA now has commissions across Italy, including hospitality and residential projects, as well as schools and a theatre. Along with a focus on reuse, especially industrial buildings, Galiotto believes that the studio’s work is united by its considered eclecticism.

“We’re influenced by art, artists, travels and whatever we can be – by curiosity,” he said. “I would say it’s something that’s very important and it gives us this kind of eclecticism. Our architecture in this moment is very eclectic and at the same time has a strong direction.”

“It’s like a piano symphony, very complicated and very up and down, but at the same time very right like a poem, very well taught and very well executed, but very complicated in terms of ingredients.”

The studio’s expanding list of projects has caused it to swell in size to approximately 30 members of staff, which Galiotto suggested is necessary to facilitate their detailed, research-led approach.

We often collaborate closely with other architects, but we are also influenced by painting, sculpture and photography which enhances the eclecticism of our projects

Looking ahead, the architects said their main objective is to continue developing their team and consolidating their approach so that others can carry it on in the coming decades.

One concern they have is maintaining the same quality of output as demand for their services grows and they take on an increasing number of projects.

In just the past year they have completed 10 projects – as many as they delivered during the first decade of their practice – with public commissions now joining their work for private clients.

Despite the rapid growth, Galiotto and Rampazzo insisted their approach remains consistent whatever scale of project they are working on, whether it’s a chair, a public plaza or a museum, which they both agree would be a dream next project.

Asked for her view on the future of architecture over the coming decades, Rampazzo said there is a trend in Italy towards involving other creatives in the design process, which represents an alternative to the more autocratic approach of the past.

“Sharing ideas and opinions leads to more interesting outcomes,” she claimed. “We often collaborate closely with other architects, but we are also influenced by painting, sculpture and photography which enhances the eclecticism of our projects.”

In their teaching roles at institutions including Kent State University and Universidade do Minho in Portugal, Galiotto and Rampazzo are responsible for helping to shape the attitudes of the next generation of architects, who they recognise are entering the workplace in challenging times.

Galiotto said if there is one thing he tries to pass on to his students and the staff in his studio it is to “have passion and to keep pushing for what you believe in.”

“If you are humble, passionate and curious then you can find success,” he added. “Sometimes it can be tough, but when you love what you do you can live your life feeling like you never worked for a single day.”

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews. The series is presented in partnership with Kohler.

In the world of movie posters, floating-head designs are among the most hated trends, and arguably no studio is more guilty of this creative sin than Marvel. Now, it seems it hasn't learned from its past, only doubling down on this disliked design with its new Doomsday poster.

Take a look at the best movie posters of all time, and you're unlikely to see a floating head. They're formulaic and overplayed, so it's no surprise that when Marvel dropped the Doomsday poster, fans understandably tore it to shreds.

Doomsday is already one of Marvel's most hyped releases since the End Game days, so you'd hope it'd bring a poster to match the energy. Instead, we've been blessed with a strange, overcrowded floating head design, muddied by an incessant shade of green.

"Bruh, this looks like the direct-to-video, bottom of the barrel s**t you saw at Walmart in 2004 and what you see on page 8 of your Prime Video search results," one scathing critic wrote. "Just ran my graphic design degree through the shredder cause nothing really matters anymore," a disgruntled designer wrote. "This is the worst poster I’ve ever seen, fan made ones are better than this trash," another added.

While it's disappointing that a huge studio like Marvel would resort to overplayed floating-head designs, previous variant designs and international posters have proved there's still creativity to be squeezed out of Marvel. (Hey, if we can't rely on the studios, there's an endless sea of fan-made poster designs that are far superior.)

#9092. YouTube Is Suddenly Obsessed With Views

This year, YouTube has changed how it counts views twice — and both occurred within three months of each other, which is shifting the paradigm of expectations for creators and advertisers. It also appears both creepy and desperate on YouTube’s part.

The first adjustment came back in August when YouTube changed when it would count a view, separating the metric into two parts: a standard view as well as an engaged view.

“A view is now defined as counting from the very first frame — whether that’s a Short appearing in the feed or a long-form video autoplaying on the Home page,” YouTube explains. “An engaged view is defined as clicking to watch or watching past the initial seconds. This has been, and will continue to be, how you qualify to earn (as long as the content is also public).”

That engaged view is basically what standard, public views were before the change and remains in place because YouTube wanted to make its view numbers appear larger to the public, but it also didn’t want to have to tie creator payouts to those higher numbers. Basically, YouTube wanted to have its cake and eat it, too.

YouTube says it changed the way it counts public views because it wanted to standardize metrics across formats and therefore measure audience reach more accurately. In short, because Meta and TikTok count views instantly on short-form content, YouTube felt like its view numbers on long-form content weren’t keeping up with the times.

This does, at least from YouTube’s perspective, make sense. Short-form has become a huge part of how people consume content now, for better or for worse. While YouTube Shorts are not nearly as popular as Instagram Reels or TikTok, YouTube does have them, and separating how it counted views there to be in line with the competition without adjusting them on long-form felt disjointed.

It’s the second view change YouTube made in 2026 that feels, as I said at the top, particularly creepy and desperate. Starting earlier this month, YouTube started estimating how many people are in the room with a viewer when they play a video on a television and counting those estimations toward the public view count.

“TVs are usually shared devices where friends, families, and communities come together to watch their favorite content. Until now, one TV playback has only counted as a single public view, even if several people watched together on the same living room screen. By updating public view counts to include co-views, we’re solving this measurement gap, better aligning with long-standing TV industry standards, and telling a more accurate story of how viewers watch your content,” YouTube says.

When first hearing how YouTube is approaching this, it sounds like YouTube is finding some way to actually see into living rooms. YouTube says this isn’t the case and it doesn’t actually know how many people are sitting in front of the television. Instead, it uses a video’s genre, audience demographics, and the time of day to guess. If YouTube thinks the video attracts a group and it is being watched in the evening, it will use that data to estimate more than one viewer.

“Co-view rate works as a ratio to show how estimated co-views contribute to your overall public views. For example, a Co-view rate of 1.10 means that for every 1,100 views of a video on TV, 1,000 are primary views from the device playback and 100 come from co-viewing,” YouTube explains.

Okay, sure, but why? It just seems like YouTube is obsessed with increasing its view counts to pump up how the platform is perceived while simultaneously not giving creators anything new. None of these changes actually affect revenue for YouTubers.

“This change only updates public view counts. Your actual creator earnings, ad revenue splits, and YouTube Partner Program (YPP) requirements remain unchanged,” YouTube stipulates regarding co-views.

That’s the part that really stands out. Sure, not giving more revenue based on the new calculation of a standard view from August makes sense. That’s not an additional person or viewer more than before; it’s just a new way of deciding at what point the view starts. Fine.

But if co-views are calculating additional people, there is no reason why those views shouldn’t count toward earned revenue. Those are, factually, additional human eyes seeing those videos.

Instead, YouTube gets to pitch advertisers on massive living-room reach while paying creators strictly on single-device clicks. Until those estimated eyeballs translate into actual ad revenue, co-views feel less like a win for creators and more like creative accounting designed to make YouTube look bigger than it is.

I guess when investors are demanding constant growth and the number of humans whose eyes can actually watch content does eventually reach a finite point, the only option is to just make up more eyes.

#9090. Nan Goldin, working mothers in the art world, new London Museum’s ancient axe head—podcast

Nan Goldin's Joey on David’s bed, Brooklyn (1999)

© Nan Goldin, courtesy the artist and Gagosian

From breaking news and insider insights to exhibitions and events around the world, the team at The Art Newspaper picks apart the art world’s big stories with the help of special guests. An award-winning podcast hosted by Ben Luke.

An exhibition at the Hayward Gallery in London is showing new and recent work by Nan Goldin. It is curated by Rachel Thomas and Ben Luke talks to her about the show.

Nan Goldin's Still from You never did anything wrong, Part I (2024)

© Nan Goldin, courtesy the artist and Gagosian

A study on motherhood and discrimination in London’s commercial art world, published by the European Journal of Cultural Studies and The Art Working Parents Alliance last week, exposes a workplace culture in which mothering children often comes at considerable professional cost. The Art Newspaper’s contributing editor Anny Shaw speaks to the authors of the report, Kate McMillan and Cleo Roberts-Komireddi.

Kate McMillan (left) and Cleo Roberts Komireddi (right)

And this episode’s Work of the Week is a Neolithic jadeite polished axehead (4000-3500 BCE). The piece is one of thousands of exhibits in the new London Museum, formally the Museum of London, the first phase of which opens this weekend in the historic General Market in Smithfield, at the heart of the City of London. Our digital editor, Alexander Morrison, discusses the axe head with Kate Sumnall, Curator of Archaeology at the museum.

We discuss Matthew Barney, Igshaan Adams, Eileen Agar and Louise Bourgeois

What’s behind the troubles facing auction houses and galleries? Plus, Sasha Skochilenko recounts her experience of being arrested—and incarcerated—in Russia, and the story behind a 1937 Surrealist painting by Ernst

Plus, a protest-themed tenth edition of the Performa Biennial and a restored portrait by Hans Holbein the Younger

It's becoming something of a tradition. Every year one of my favourite items in my house, the Moccamaster Select coffee maker, gets a nice discount for Black Friday, and I tell you all to buy it because it's a beautiful object and, almost as importantly, it makes delicious coffee. Welcome to the 2026 edition.

Moccamaster has knocked 33% of its entire range of Select coffee makers at Amazon, bringing the price of the KBGV model down from $369 to $247.95. That's a massive saving of $122 – and one that I'm frankly furious to have missed out on myself. (Muggins over here paid full price for the thing in 2022.)

Save $122: You can currently save 33% on Technivorm's flagship Moccamaster coffee maker. This pump-free coffee maker heats water to the correct temperature for coffee extraction, brewing a full 40 oz pot of coffee in 4-6 minutes using one switch.

Meanwhile, the KBT model, which features a manually adjustable drip-stop, is also 33% off, down from $349 to $233. This version offers a little more control over how fast coffee flows into the carafe.

So why the fuss? Well, for a start, the KBGV is a design classic that's been keeping us caffeinated since 1974. In short, it's the Rolls-Royce of coffee makers. It's almost worth it for the design alone – this thing wouldn't look out of place in a kitchen from any of the last five decades.

And if the fact that I'm a fan of the Moccamaster isn't enough to convince you that it's a design classic, what about Gwyneth Paltrow? According to Homes & Gardens, the Goopster swears by it too.

#9088. HTA Design unveils "UK's largest council housing development"

A collection of brick-clad buildings containing over 450 homes forms Kidbrooke Park Road in London, which architecture studio HTA Design claims is the largest new-build council housing development in the UK.

Built on a formerly disused site in Greenwich, the development contains 452 homes, all of which are social housing.

Construction company Durkan delivered Kidbrooke Park Road for the Royal Borough of Greenwich as part of its council housing programme, Greenwich Builds.

HTA Design said the project “demonstrates what can be achieved when local authorities take an ambitious approach to housing delivery”.

“Our main goal was to demonstrate that council housing delivered at scale does not have to come at the expense of good design,” HTA Design managing partner Simon Bayliss told Dezeen.

“We wanted to create a neighbourhood where the homes are generous and adaptable, where landscape is integral rather than an afterthought, and where streets and public spaces feel active, welcoming and safe,” he continued.

“Together, the two phases have delivered the UK’s largest council housing development and one of the most significant social housing projects completed in recent years. We hope it serves as a benchmark for how future generations of affordable housing can be delivered across London and the UK.”

HTA Design recently completed the second phase of the scheme, which adds eight housing blocks with 330 homes to the three blocks completed in phase one.

Ranging from six to 15 storeys, the housing comprises one-, two-, and three-bedroom apartments and family maisonettes, most of which are dual-aspect.

The buildings at Kidbrooke Park Road have a reinforced concrete frame, clad in brick chosen to reference red-brick buildings in the local area.

Arched entrances, patterned brickwork and exposed concrete elements were designed to add visual interest among the development’s green spaces, which include tree-lined streets, community gardens, wildflower meadows, play areas and gardens designed for rainwater runoff.

“A key challenge was ensuring that two phases delivered separately would ultimately come together as one place,” said Bayliss.

“Through simple buildings and typologies with repetitive architectural components, combined with a landscape strategy that runs throughout the development, we set out to create a neighbourhood with a clear identity that worked within its context.”

Elsewhere in the development are a nursery, community facilities and green roofs. The housing is complete with air-source heat pumps, electric boilers and rooftop photovoltaics.

“We hope residents feel proud to live here,” Bayliss concluded.

“Beyond the homes themselves, the project has been designed to support everyday life, with play spaces, shared green areas, a nursery, community facilities and local amenities all contributing to a strong sense of community,” he said.

“Those are often the things that transform a housing development into a genuine neighbourhood.”

The deputy mayor of London for Housing and Residential Development Tom Copley said the project represents how London is “leading the way nationally on council home building”.

“The new development at Kidbrooke Park Road is the perfect example of what we’re achieving, with 452 council homes forming the largest single entirely new-build council housing development in the country,” he said.

“We recently announced that 60 per cent of the funding from the first round of the mayor’s new Social and Affordable Homes Programme will go to London boroughs, and we look forward to that decision delivering even more new council homes in future.”

Last month, the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) announced the brick-clad Lion Green Road housing by Mary Duggan Architects with Ruff Architects, which contains a mix of private and socially rented homes, as the winner of this year’s Stirling Prize.

RIBA also awarded its Neave Brown Award for Housing to Rowan Court, a cluster of brick-clad social housing blocks in Seven Sisters designed by Satish Jassal Architects.

#9087. These Awards Celebrate the Very Best Adventure and Action Sports Photography

These Awards Celebrate the Very Best Adventure and Action Sports Photography

The category winners for the Illume Awards have been revealed, an extreme sports photography competition built on the legacy of Red Bull Illume.

For 20 years, Red Bull turned the Illume Awards into the most recognizable competition for adventure and action sports photography.

This year, it is just the Illume Awards. But the breathtaking images keep coming; check out this year’s category winners below.

French photographer Louis Garnier has won the Snow Category of The Illume Awards 2026 with his photo of skier Kevin Rolland captured in front of a fire fountain in Tignes, France.

“The energy around the whole project was incredible. We only had three attempts with the flames, and it is still my favorite photo I’ve ever made with Kevin”, he recounts about the day the winning photo was taken.

Austrian photographer Tom Klocker takes the title in the Climb Category with his photograph of climber Mario Andexlinger in Iceland, selected as the winning image from 20 Climb Category Finalists.

“This shot was very challenging, and you had to have extremely good ice climbing experience. The mystical atmosphere that day went perfectly with the colors,” says Klocker about the making of the photograph.

French photographer Tim Rochas has won the Aerial Category of The Illume Awards 2026 with his photograph of paraglider Pierre Bottero flying alongside Factory Butte in Utah, United States.

Captured from another glider in flight, the image places the pilot against the vast, rugged desert landscape, creating a striking contrast between the scale of nature and the small human presence in the air.

The story behind the winning photograph began with a flight from the top of Factory Butte. As the pilots took to the air above the extraordinary desert landscape, Rochas saw an opportunity to capture Bottero alongside the immense rock formation.

“For me, this image is about the contrast between the fragility of a human in flight and the raw power of nature,” he says.

Portuguese photographer Beatriz Ryder is the winner of the Surf Category of The Illume Awards 2026. Her photograph of surfer Shaley Mercado in the Solomon Islands was selected as the winning image from 20 Surf Category Finalists.

“We were in one of the most remote parts of the world, the Solomon Islands. Right in front of where we were staying was this little wave – shallow, fast, and with short, fun runners,” says Ryder about the location behind her winning photograph.

Spanish photographer Ágata Dominguez has won the Trail Category of The Illume Awards 2026 with her captivating photo of late athlete Ida Amelie Robsahm captured in Sancti Spiritu, Spain, during the Zegama-Aizkorri Race 2026, a legendary trail running race.

“What I love most about photography is being there for the moments that are difficult to explain afterwards, capturing that look, that movement, and that energy in a split second: the tension, the concentration, and the feeling of being completely immersed in what’s happening. I’m not just interested in getting the perfect shot; I would like my images to make you feel something and, ideally, make you feel like you were there,” she explains her approach to photography.

German photographer Robert Christ takes the title in the Skate Category with his photograph of skater André Gerlich in Germany, selected as the winning image from 20 Skate Category Finalists.

Robert Christ’s photo captures André Gerlich performing a backside air trick on a sculpture by Andreas Kiessling in southern Germany.

“André and I found out about a sculpture bike path and immediately made plans to go there. André chose to skate this rough piece of concrete, did a stylish backside air, and we got a photo we were both really stoked about,” Christ says.

American photographer Lear Miller has won the Bike Category of The Illume Awards 2026 with his photograph of Hannah Bergemann, captured as part of Chris Benchetler’s Mountains of the Moon project in Pacific City, Oregon, United States.

Getting the photo was not easy, as Miller explains, “We shot the bike segment of Chris Benchetler’s Mountains of the Moon over four nights, from about 10 pm to 4 am, in some pretty brutal rain. The riders were riding in the dark while we constantly battled water on the lenses and gear.”

Chilean photographer Gonzalo Robert Parraguez has been named the winner of the Adventure Category of The Illume Awards 2026 with his photograph of kayaker Aniol Serrasolses in Svalbard, Norway.

The photo captures Aniol Serrasolses descending a waterfall in the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard.

“We always talk about the photo, but we rarely talk about the athletes, and I dedicate this 100% to Aniol; he was the one who pushed for this whole project to happen, so that we could be taking these incredible photos in the middle of the Arctic”, says Parraguez.

For more on the contest, head to the Illume Awards website.

#9086. Missouri Investigates Photographer After Customers Say They Never Received Images

Missouri Investigates Photographer After Customers Say They Never Received Images

Missouri has opened an investigation into a photography business after allegedly leaving numerous customers without the pictures they paid for or a refund.

According to a report by First Alert 4, Leave It to Beaver Photography — a professional family, newborn and wedding photography business based in Wentzville, Missouri — announced it had closed this week after 13 years in business.

However, numerous customers have contacted First Alert 4 with complaints about the company. Some allege they paid for photography services covering events such as weddings, births and anniversaries, but never received their photographs or a refund.

Kristen Moran alleges she hired Leave It to Beaver Photography to take family photographs during a Memorial Day weekend camping trip. She also contracted the company for a maternity shoot in July.

Moran said the photographs were supposed to be delivered within 20 days, but they did not arrive as promised.

“It came to months and months of her saying oh I have them, don’t worry about it. Just kind of getting the runaround,” Moran tells the news outlet.

Moran said the photographs eventually arrived in late October, but by then she had already given birth and no longer needed the maternity images.

“Late October she did send me the photos. She sent me like 300 of them. I was like okay, great. They’re not really relevant anymore, I already had my baby,” Moran says.

In another case, Monica Dannegger alleges she hired Leave It to Beaver Photography to photograph her wedding on December 12, 2026. Dannegger says she paid the business $1,500, representing half the cost of photographing her wedding and an engagement party. However, she alleges the photographer did not attend the engagement party and that she has received no communication about the wedding. Dannegger also says she has been unable to obtain a refund.

“It’s unfortunate that her end of the bargain isn’t being upheld,” Dannegger tells First Alert 4. “I would have been left high and dry.”

The Missouri attorney general has reportedly opened an investigation into the photography business, which operates in St. Charles County. The office is encouraging customers who believe they have been affected to file a complaint through its website. Wentzville police have also advised customers who paid for services they did not receive to file a police report. Officers say they will investigate.

First Alert 4 says it had contacted Leave It to Beaver Photography for comment but had been unable to reach the photographer.

The news comes a wedding photographer was ordered to pay $1.7 million by the North Carolina Attorney General after leaving hundreds of customers without the services they paid for.

Picture this: you're stepping off a direct overnight flight at Dublin Airport, passport in hand, ready to spend two weeks exploring Ireland's Wild Atlantic Way — and the transatlantic crossing that would have cost you $600 per seat cost you just 13,000 Avios instead. That's the moment this redemption delivers. For the ChooseFI community, the math here is almost offensive in how good it is. A round-trip economy ticket from Boston to Dublin on Aer Lingus typically runs $300–$600 per person, and during peak summer travel it can climb even higher. At 13,000 Avios one-way, you're squeezing **2.3 to 4.6 cents per point** out of every Avios you redeem. To put that in perspective, most loyalty program analysts consider 1.5 cents per point a solid redemption. You're potentially tripling that benchmark on what is genuinely one of the easiest award bookings in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. The pricing inefficiency here runs deep. British Airways uses a **distance-based award chart** — meaning the price in Avios is determined by how many miles the plane physically flies, not by what the airline thinks the market will bear on that route. The North Atlantic crossing from the U.S. East Coast to Ireland is, by aviation standards, a relatively short haul. Dublin sits closer to Boston than Los Angeles does. That geographic reality, baked into BA's award chart structure, means you pay a "short-haul" price for what most travelers consider a major international trip. Aer Lingus operates modern Airbus A321LR aircraft on these transatlantic routes — a genuine premium product in economy with dedicated transatlantic seating, meal service, and that unmistakably warm Irish hospitality. This isn't a cramped regional jet. You're flying a purpose-built transatlantic cabin at a fraction of the cash cost. For a family of four, this redemption is transformational. At 13,000 Avios per person each way, a family round trip costs 104,000 Avios total — a points balance that's achievable with a single well-timed credit card welcome bonus. The alternative? Dropping $2,400 or more in cash for the same four seats. That's real money that stays in your FI journey.

The core insight here is understanding what British Airways Avios actually prices — and exploiting the gap between that and what the market charges.

BA's Avios program uses a distance-based award chart. Every flight is assigned a price based on the number of miles between the origin and destination, broken into distance bands. The critical band for this redemption is the one covering flights up to approximately 2,000 miles for partner airlines. Boston (BOS) to Dublin (DUB) clocks in at roughly 3,100 miles — but here's where it gets interesting: Aer Lingus prices these transatlantic short-haul routes within a favorable partner tier that makes the Avios cost dramatically lower than you'd ever pay booking directly.

Layer 1 — You're not booking BA flights. You're using BA Avios to book Aer Lingus flights. This distinction is everything. British Airways-operated long-haul flights carry notoriously high fuel surcharges — often $300–$800 or more on top of the Avios cost, which can completely destroy the value of your redemption. Aer Lingus, as a partner airline, charges no fuel surcharges on Avios bookings. You pay the Avios plus modest government taxes and fees, typically $5–$30. That's it.

Layer 2 — Off-peak pricing drops it further. BA Avios has off-peak pricing for Aer Lingus transatlantic routes, and when you travel in shoulder season, the rate can be even more favorable. The ChooseFI community travels smart: avoiding peak summer crowds and booking shoulder seasons isn't just about lower prices, it's about a better experience overall.

The instant transfer speeds from Chase, Amex, and Bilt mean you can search for availability, confirm your seats, then transfer points — no need to speculatively move points weeks in advance. That flexibility is a significant advantage for planning.

One important program nuance: Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. As long as you earn or redeem at least once every three years, your balance stays alive. For most ChooseFI members who hold a Chase or Amex card and regularly earn points, this is a non-issue — but it's worth knowing before you let a balance sit dormant.

Before transferring a single point, verify that award space actually exists on your target dates. Navigate to aerlingus.com and search for flights on your route (Boston, New York JFK, or Chicago ORD to Dublin). Aer Lingus displays Avios availability directly on their website — look for the "Avios" fare option when selecting your flight. This is the cleanest way to confirm seats before committing your points.

Alternatively, log into your British Airways Executive Club account at ba.com and use their award search tool. Search for Aer Lingus flights between your U.S. city and Dublin. The results will show Avios pricing — what you're looking for is the off-peak rate, which will display as lower Avios than the standard/peak option.

Use the BA award calendar view to spot off-peak pricing. Generally, traveling outside of peak summer (late June through August) and major holidays will unlock the best Avios rates. Shoulder seasons — late September through November and February through mid-April — are where the ChooseFI community finds the sweet spot of lower crowds, lower prices, and still-beautiful Irish weather.

Once you've confirmed availability on your target dates, calculate the total Avios needed: 13,000 per person, per direction. For a round trip for two, that's 52,000 Avios. Don't transfer until you're ready to book immediately.

Aer Lingus awards do carry fuel surcharges, typically $100-$200 round trip in economy. While not zero, this is still dramatically less than the $500-$1,000+ cash fare. The net savings remain substantial despite the surcharges.

Dublin can serve as an excellent gateway to the rest of Europe. Aer Lingus offers connections to many European cities from Dublin, and you can also book separate budget airline flights within Europe. Additionally, Dublin has U.S. Preclearance, meaning you clear customs before your return flight — a rare convenience.

Search on the British Airways website (ba.com) using the "Book with Avios" option. Enter your departure city and Dublin as the destination. Aer Lingus-operated flights will appear alongside any BA-operated options. Availability is best 4-10 months in advance.

This redemption was practically designed for families taking their first international trip on points. The scores tell the story: 5/5 for both Family Friendly and Beginner Friendly. Here's why.

At 13,000 Avios per person per direction, a family of four round trip requires 104,000 Avios — a balance achievable with one or two credit card welcome bonuses. The process of booking is straightforward, the availability is genuinely good (4/5), and there are no complicated routing rules to navigate. If your family has been thinking about Ireland and has a Chase or Amex card with a points balance, this is your gateway.

Couples planning a European trip will find this equally compelling — 52,000 Avios for a round trip for two is a realistic near-term savings goal.

Solo travelers with smaller Avios balances can book one-way legs and mix with other redemptions — fly to Dublin on Avios, return from Lisbon on a separate award, and build a multi-country European trip.

This redemption is not ideal for travelers who are highly inflexible on dates and must travel in peak summer. While availability is good, peak summer award space can be tighter. It's also not the right tool for someone trying to fly business class transatlantic — this sweet spot is economy-class only, and the Aer Lingus business class product ("Business Class" cabin) prices considerably higher.

Minimum to get started: 13,000 Avios for a one-way, 26,000 for a round trip solo. Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One Miles, and Bilt points all transfer at 1:1.

This redemption earns its **"Easy" / "Beginner" rating** honestly — and here's specifically why. The three things that make award bookings hard are: earning enough points, finding availability, and navigating a complex booking process. This sweet spot sidesteps all three. **Earning is accessible**: The points requirement (13,000 per direction) is low enough that a single credit card welcome bonus provides multiple round trips. You're not chasing exotic transfer partners or waiting years to accumulate. **Availability is genuinely good**: Aer Lingus releases reasonable Avios award space on their transatlantic routes, especially in shoulder season. You're not fighting for one or two seats on a sold-out flight — the calendar will show multiple options. **Booking is clean and predictable**: The BA website is functional, transfers from Chase and Amex arrive instantly (no speculative transfers required), and Aer Lingus imposes no fuel surcharges on partner bookings. The experience is: search, confirm space, transfer, book. Done. **The one thing to watch**: New members sometimes inadvertently book BA-metal connecting flights instead of direct Aer Lingus flights — and then encounter surprise fuel surcharges. The fix is simple: always verify your flight number starts with "EI" (Aer Lingus) and not "BA." When in doubt, search directly on aerlingus.com first to confirm the flight, then book through BA's award portal. If you've never booked an award flight before, this is an ideal first redemption. The systems are forgiving, the value is immediately obvious, and the destination — Ireland — will make you a believer in the travel rewards lifestyle for years to come.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

The BA Avios sweet spot to Dublin on Aer Lingus is one of the most compelling transatlantic redemptions available. At 13,000 Avios each way for a nonstop flight that regularly costs $500-$1,000+ in cash, the value proposition is hard to beat. Even with fuel surcharges of $100-$200 round trip, the total cost of 26,000 Avios plus modest fees dramatically undercuts the cash fare. With four major transfer partners and multiple East Coast departure cities, this sweet spot is accessible and practical. If Europe is on your travel list, Dublin via Aer Lingus should be one of the first routes you explore.

#9083. Leica Introduces Two New Camera Bags Made by Billingham

Leica Introduces Two New Camera Bags Made by Billingham

Leica has partnered with British camera bag manufacturer Billingham to introduce two new camera bags designed specifically for its mirrorless cameras.

The new bags come in two sizes: a compact version designed for the Leica M and Q cameras, and a larger model intended for the Leica SL system, such as this year’s Leica SL3-P. Both feature interiors tailored to their respective camera systems, with space for a camera with an attached lens and an additional lens.

Each bag also includes dedicated pockets for SD and CFexpress cards, an internal mesh pocket for accessories, and customizable dividers to keep equipment organized and accessible. An exterior strap allows the bags to be attached to a luggage trolley, making them easier to transport when traveling.

Both models are manufactured in the U.K. using Billingham’s FibreNyte, a proprietary waterproof synthetic material, combined with leather detailing. The bags are available in three color combinations: black, sage/black, and khaki/chocolate.

The Billingham for Leica M/Q bag and Billingham for Leica SL bag will be available from today (November 26, 2026) at selected Leica stores worldwide and through the Leica online store.

The M/Q model has a recommended retail price of £300 ($395) / €350, while the larger SL version costs £380 ($500) / €450.

#9082. Comment | The future of the ancient city of Palmyra should be determined by its local community

The Syrian antiquities department’s efforts to restore Palmyra—a Unesco World Heritage Site since 1980—are progressing again

The ancient city of Palmyra in Syria rose to the world’s attention in May 2015, when Isis militants occupied the site. Within five months, they had destroyed the Temple of Baalshamin, the Temple of Bel, and the Arch of Triumph—all 2,000-year-old masterpieces. That same year, their murder of Khaled al-Asaad, Palmyra’s retired head of antiquities, sparked worldwide outrage.

In the wake of these atrocities, institutions and governments around the globe launched a dizzying array of projects. Many focused on preserving the site digitally: the University of California San Diego Library reconstructed the Temple of Bel, for example, and the Université de Lausanne did likewise for the Temple of Baalshamin. Others aimed to one day physically reconstruct what had been lost, including a Russian project to restore the Arch of Triumph. But by the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024, none of these plans had been realised.

Now under a new government, the Syrian antiquities department’s efforts to restore Palmyra—a Unesco World Heritage Site since 1980—are again progressing. It has been working to remove illegal constructions and stop illegal excavations, while Palmyra’s local community has been engaged in cleaning the museum’s gardens, among other projects. Meanwhile, a Heritage for Peace project is evaluating the structural condition of buildings in Palmyra’s modern city, which had a pre-war population of 70,000. This renewed momentum once again raises an important question: to what extent should Palmyra’s ancient ruins be physically reconstructed, if at all?

Archaeologist Nour A. Munawar of the University of Amsterdam addressed this problem in 2017, while the war still raged. He emphasised that whether or not to reconstruct should be a decision for Palmyra’s local community, irrespective of where they now live or their political views. Writing in Ex Noxo Journal of Archaeology, he warns that previous reconstruction projects largely left communities out of discussions—such as the limited local consultation when the Stari Most bridge was rebuilt in Mostar, Bosnia and Herzegovina, or how commercial buildings dominated the reconstruction of post-war Beirut. There is also the danger of “Disneyfication”, a label for artificial, over-polished reconstructions.

Whether to reconstruct has long been a dilemma for war-ravaged places. I recently visited Ypres, Belgium, a city that was totally destroyed during the First World War. In the aftermath, some wondered whether it should be rebuilt as it once appeared, or if its old architecture should be replaced with something more modern. Winston Churchill was in favour of leaving it untouched, as a memorial to the horrors of war. In the end, the local people made the decision: they wanted their Medieval town rebuilt—even if, for the most part, only the facades reflected the pre-war era.

A 2024 study by Benjamin Isakhan, a professor of international politics at Deakin University, Melbourne, and Lynn Meskell, a professor of anthropology at the University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, provides an insight into how Syrians feel about this issue. After surveying 1,600 Aleppo residents, they found that almost all were proud of their cultural heritage, but Aleppines prioritised “safety and security”, “electricity, water and other services” and “unemployment and poverty” over “heritage protection and reconstruction” in terms of urgency.

And although 98% agreed that damaged or destroyed heritage sites should be restored or reconstructed, opinions varied on how: 17% wanted them to appear as “first built”, 24% as they appeared before the war, and 30% wanted them “restored and reconstructed into a new and more modern structure”. Heritage experts’ preference for authenticity could therefore go against some local wishes. Overwhelmingly, Aleppines also wanted Syrian control over rebuilding their heritage, not global agencies, NGOs, and foreign governments, Isakhan and Meskell note in the International Journal of Heritage Studies.

Palmyra is now a symbol of Syria, known worldwide. But whether the city’s rebuilt heritage retains its battle scars, becomes “Disneyfied”, or something in between, should be a local choice, as should whether any reconstruction is prioritised over more pressing needs. As time passes, an increasing number of voices will come into play—the new Syrian government, foreign governments, international bodies, NGOs and cultural heritage experts—all providing much-needed money, aid and advice. We must hope that the local community is not lost in the mix. In the end, it must be the people of Palmyra who decide their city’s fate.

#9081. Estudio A-G uses colour to update 1960s book-lined house in Mexico City

Photography by Leandro Bulzzano, Ricardo Letona

Local studio Estudio A-G has foregrounded a sculptural timber structural element while implementing bold colours for the renovation of a 1960s house in Mexico City.

Originally built in 1962 by Jaime Ortiz Monasterio, Casa Magnolia is located in the residential neighbourhood of San Ángel.

Monasterio designed the home as a domestic library for his brother, who was an avid reader and book collector. Over the decades, the house was renovated multiple times, obscuring the home’s original character.

In 2025, Andrés Gutiérrez, head of Estudio A-G, was commissioned to reinterpret the interior of the 275-square-metre residence for new inhabitants, preserving the architectural qualities that made the original design unique.

“The restoration was extremely respectful of the house’s original architecture, but we never wanted the result to feel nostalgic,” Gutiérrez told Dezeen.

“Quite the opposite – once restored, the house needed to feel completely new, fresh and contemporary, which was exactly what the clients were looking for.”

Completed in February 2026, the design uses colour to achieve the transformation, bringing new energy to the original architecture without competing with it. The studio aimed to have the house be recognisably Mexican without falling into tropes.

“I wanted the house to feel unmistakably Mexican, but without relying on folklore or the usual clichés associated with ‘Mexican interiors’.” he said.

“I was much more interested in expressing that identity through materials, craftsmanship, colour and contemporary Mexican design.”

At the centre of the house, a dark-toned timber structure rises through a series of split levels like a sculptural tree connecting the entrance hall, living room, dining room, study and reading areas before unfolding into a double-height ceiling.

“More than a structural element, it serves as a spatial anchor, establishing continuity throughout the interior and reinforcing the vertical dimension of the house,” Gutiérrez said, explaining that wood acts as a warm, unifying element throughout the house.

The studio restored and reintegrated the original wood flooring, ceiling finishes and structural elements. It also reinstalled most of the original wooden bookshelves that had been dismantled and stored.

“Overall, the intervention focused on restoring the elements that were worth preserving while introducing the necessary contemporary updates to make the house fully functional for the way its new owners live today,” he said.

The studio replaced some window frames and all the glass, updated the lighting and electrical systems and rebuilt the bathrooms and kitchen.

However, one of the most significant interventions were the colour blocks and new materials included in the space.

“Colour plays a central role in the project,” Gutiérrez said, calling out soft blue walls that are a backdrop for deep plum sofas, moss green dining chairs, lilac rugs, green serpentine stone and terracotta-toned marble.

“Rather than acting as decoration, colour is used as an architectural tool to organise space, establish hierarchy, and shape atmosphere.”

He also designed custom furniture that pairs with historic pieces – like Antonio Attolini’s 1969 armchairs – and contemporary Mexican art. Works by Cecilia Barreto, Francisco Muñoz, Jorge Rosano, Daniel Berman and Adriana Silva embed culture into everyday life.

Previously, Estudio A-G designed a rooftop bar as a “matriarchal universe,” complete with crocodile-shaped furniture and shrine-like water, for a boutique hotel in a former Spanish colonial manor house in San Miguel de Allende.

#9080. How a Photographer Got a Credit on Jennifer Lopez’s Instagram Account

How a Photographer Got a Credit on Jennifer Lopez’s Instagram Account

A photographer has revealed how he managed to get a credit on Jennifer Lopez’s Instagram account after the star initially reposted his video without any attribution.

Los Angeles-based David Christopher Lee has been a celebrity portrait photographer for 27 years, capturing stars like Lady Gaga, the Kardashians, and Britney Spears.

On November 19, Lee attended the premiere of Jennifer Lopez’s The JLo Show at Paramount Studios in Hollywood as a guest of his friend Maximillian Acevedo. Lee says he had no intentions of taking any photographs or videos at the event.

However, when Lopez came out on the red carpet, photographers rushed out to take pictures, and Lee couldn’t resist shooting some images of the star herself. Lee moved behind the crowd of photographers to find a different angle of Lopez. He noticed Lopez’s yellow diamond necklace and zoomed in to capture a 13-second video on his iPhone at 5x zoom.

The lighting was particularly good, illuminating Lopez’s jawline and earring, and Lee says he immediately knew he had captured the shot he wanted.

“As all the photographers started calling her name. I bolted for the red carpet and stood in the back looking for the perfect angle and whipped out my iPhone, shooting it on 5x,” Lee tells PetaPixel. “My eyes immediately went to her necklace so I framed it like a jewelry shot and the rest is history. I posted the video immediately on Instagram and it immediately went viral.”

Lee posted the video to his Instagram account (@davidsguide) at 6:25 PM that day. A few hours later, Lopez’s own Instagram account reposted Lee’s clip to her 239 million followers without crediting or tagging him.

Lee initially did not realize Lopez had reposted his video because the sound was different. But he eventually recognized his camera movement.

“At first I didn’t know it was my video because the sound was different,” Lee says. “Then I noticed the same movement of my camera and compared them side by side. I was in shock that she had posted it to her 239 million followers, the only video from that night.”

Lee says he felt both pleased that his video had gone viral and upset that it was shared without credit, leaving viewers unaware he had filmed it.

“Out of the 100 photographers and videographers there, she had posted my video. I was sad and happy at the same time,” Lee explains. “The video was getting millions of views, and nobody knew I shot it. I felt violated because I’m entertainment, the least someone can do is credit you for using your content.”

Rather than let the video circulate without credit, Lee took matters into his own hands, contacting several members of Lopez’s team before reaching her social media manager, who agreed to credit his work.

“I reached out to everyone I could find on her team and finally got in touch with her social media manager after five million views,” Lee tells PetaPixel. “I emailed him asking him to credit, and within ten minutes, he replied sorry and gave credit in the video. I felt so accomplished at that point.”

As of writing, Lopez’s repost, which now includes Lee’s Instagram tag @davidcleephotography, has over 350,000 likes and over 9,600 comments. Lee says that reposting content without attribution can give it a wide audience while leaving the original photographer unrecognized. He believes photographers frequently have their work shared without credit because content spreads so quickly online that people sometimes forget to acknowledge its creator.

“It happens all the time,” Lee says. “Content moves and travels so fast these days that a lot of times people forget to tag and credit. It is unfortunate, but it’s the world we live in.”

Lee encourages photographers to learn from his experience and take precautions when sharing their work on social media. He advises them to watermark their images and videos before posting, as they never know how widely the content might be shared.

“The lesson is you never know what can happen with your content and the best thing to do is watermark your pics or videos before posting,” Lee says.

He adds: “Keep doing what you do and do stop believing in yourself. The possibilities are endless.”

More of David Christopher’s work can be found on his website and blog David’s Guide.

Like lots of parents, I'm always looking for activities that stop my kids sitting sedentary in front of screens. I use all the tech-free tactics I can, like arts and crafts and board games, but I also value the experiences tech can give them. I just want that tech to be more creative than a tablet or the TV.

Not all kids' tech is evil, and some is pretty darn great. I've found a niche that combines being a parent, my love of design and my years as an early years teacher, and it means I get to test some seriously good products. There are a few I'm firmly recommending, and they'd make great Christmas presents.

I love the Yoto. I can't shout about this enough. We've been using it for the last seven years, I bought one when my daughter was two, and it's going from strength to strength in functionality and design (read my interview with the team who recently redesigned the hardware). The Yoto does have a screen but is very deliberately only using it to display fun pixel graphics, and the time.

If you're not familiar, you play stories and music hosted on cards via the Yoto machine – which comes in a full sized and mini version. Cards are available to buy – but you can also make your own cards, which is the major selling point for me. You can record your own content, or you can put MP3 files onto them. There's also an ever-changing library of podcasts and other audio, accessed via an app.

Yoto is currently up to 30% off – and it would make a fabulous Christmas present.

I bang on about the Nex Playground to everyone – my family adores it. It's an active play system that gets players up and moving through its whole body tracking. In my experience, this console counters the usual effect video games or tablets have on children. It encourages discussion, collaboration with its gentle and imaginative games, which include sports like Bowling (my son's favourite), and big-name titles like How to Train Your Dragon and Bluey. See our full Nex Playground review here.

If you're thinking about a console for your children this Christmas, I really can't recommend this one enough – and it's also currently got 37% in the UK, and 30% in the US off for Black Friday.

If you've got a younger child interested in 3D printing, this is a great option. As I say in my Funbox review, if your child is at the upper end of the 4-12 age bracket, I'd go for a proper 3D printer. My daughter is on the borderline at 9, but my son (5) would get plenty of life from this printer.

It's a fun design, and is super-simple to use via an app. You can draw designs and let the AI print them, or pick from a marketplace of designs (make sure you use the official UGEE designs for maximum effectiveness). Because it's enclosed, it's safer for kids to use.

It's currently got a small saving of $20 at Amazon.

This is the one I'm yet to try, but I'm so excited by the idea. I join a lot of parents in not wanting my children to have their own phones for a long while yet, but I realised that when I was younger I would be phoning my friends on the landline. We don't have a landline, and I gatekeep my own phone for obvious reasons. So I was searching for a solution – and the Tin Can is perfect.

Pitched as a New-School Landline phone, it connects to the WiFi and only phones/accepts calls from approved numbers (controlled via an app). If another child has a TinCan, they can phone each other for free, and other approved numbers can be called if you pay a monthly subscription.

I've got one on its way to me so I'll be doing a review on it soon, but I wanted to put it on your radar as I think it's such a smart idea. It's out in the US, and preorders are open for before-Christmas delivery in the UK.

#9078. Investigation Reveals Who Betrayed Photographer Secretly Documenting Nazi-Occupied France

Investigation Reveals Who Betrayed Photographer Secretly Documenting Nazi-Occupied France

A new investigation has uncovered how a brave photographer, who risked his life taking hundreds of pictures of Nazi-occupied France, may have been betrayed by two neighbors.

In April 2020, a mysterious album containing hundreds of photos of daily life during the German Nazi occupation of Paris from 1940 to 1942 was discovered in a flea market in Barjac in Gard, France.

Raoul Minot.1940-42. Paris occupé WW2 pic.twitter.com/SBnUj87HWA

— Paris Paname (@ParisAMDParis) August 24, 2024

Le Monde journalist Philippe Broussard began a four-year investigation to identify the photographer, who had taken at least 700 pictures of Paris during the first two years of the Occupation. At the time, unauthorized photography was banned by the Nazis, and taking such pictures could carry the death penalty. In 2024, Broussard identified the photographer as Raoul Minot.

Minot used a “little Kodak Brownie 6/9 camera” and developed the prints in the photographic laboratory of the department store where he worked. He then sold hundreds of his images to the French Resistance, a collection of groups that fought against the Nazi occupation during World War II.

However, Minot’s photographic mission came to an end in November 1942, just two years after it began, when an unidentified informer reported his activities to the Nazis.

Minot was imprisoned and deported to Mauthausen concentration camp in Austria on April 20, 1943, where he was forced to perform labor. He was later transferred to Flossenbürg concentration camp in Bavaria and liberated by U.S. forces on April 23, 1945. He tragically died five days later in a hospital in Cham, Bavaria.

Following his discovery of Minot in 2024, Broussard set out to uncover who had turned in the photographer to the Nazis for a report in Le Monde. A breakthrough came in April 2026, when a reader contacted Le Monde with a document that could help solve the mystery. Jean-Pierre Gross, a local history enthusiast from Courbevoie, France, had discovered a 1944 report accusing two of Minot’s neighbors, Marie Breux and Georges Robinson, of collaborating with the Germans and helping secure the arrests of people suspected of opposing the Occupation.

The report specifically named Minot, stating that the couple were suspected of having “denounced or, at the very least, incriminated” him. It also claimed they had boasted about getting 18 people arrested.

Breux was the building’s concierge, while Robinson, her partner, was a tailor with a history of theft and other criminal convictions. Both were arrested following the Liberation in August 1944, although no record of a conviction against either has been found.

Further investigation revealed that Robinson had briefly worked at the same Printemps department store as Minot, potentially explaining how he knew about the store’s photographic facilities.

Broussard later uncovered an anonymous letter sent in December 1942 that accused Minot and his wife of photographing Nazi propaganda posters and bomb damage. The letter prompted a police investigation that led to Minot’s arrest and the seizure of more than 1,000 photographic negatives.

“Sir, could you ask the Minot household, both of whom work at the Printemps — the wife as a cashier, the husband as a warehouse manager — whether their jobs qualify them to take photographs of propaganda posters and air raid damage to our poor country?” the letter reads. “We don’t think it would be very useful to inform you about the troubled times France is going through, thanks to many workers in troubled waters.

According to Le Monde, a handwriting expert subsequently ruled out Robinson as the author of the anonymous letter that triggered the investigation into Minot, but could not exclude Breux. Broussard believes the couple may have worked together to report Minot after discovering that he was photographing Nazi propaganda posters and bomb damage around Courbevoie.

Although there is still no conclusive evidence to establish who sent the letter, Broussard’s investigation has brought researchers closer than ever to identifying the people who may have brought Minot’s secret photographic mission to an end.
