#9060. Comment | Cop31 may have faltered but, as grassroots initiatives in the art world and beyond remind us‚ all is not lost

This year's United Nations Climate Change Conference, known as Cop31, concluded with no deal on Sunday, 22 November, two days after it was set to close

In this monthly column, Louisa Buck looks at how the art world is responding to the environmental and climate crisis.

The fact that Cop31 failed to reach a final agreement on tackling climate change is obviously cause for grave concern. Despite the talks in Antalya, Turkey running over by two days as delegates struggled to achieve a consensus, they were ultimately derailed by the refusal by a group of oil producing states—led by Saudi Arabia and including Russia—to allow any mention of fossil fuel in the conference’s final agreement. This despite an agreement already made at Cop28 in 2023 to “transition away” from coal, oil and gas. As a result, more than 130 countries, including the European Union (EU) and the UK, refused to sign off a deal which omitted any reference to the main cause of climate change.

“We will not accept a Cop that greenwashes fossil fuel”, declared the EU representative Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s minister for climate, environment and energy, also stating that a climate pact which makes no mention of fossil fuel was “unconscionable” and “failed to meet the moment.”

Much of the art on display at Cop also seemed out of kilter with the urgency of the times. The centrepiece of the official CopArt programme, which was installed across the Cop site and curated by art advisor and contemporary art curator Nagihan Ozel, was an extensive installation of 18 mirror panels installed in the Green Zone and created by veteran artist Heinz Mack who has been making similar work since the 1960s. Other conspicuous pieces included Anselm Kiefer’s giant seascape bearing a pair of metal scales, Für Rabbi Löw (2010-12) and a forest made from recycled cardboard from Eva Jospin. Two monumental bronze sculptures by Belgian artist Koen Vanmechelen, one of an ape standing on a mirrored glass sphere balanced on a human thumb and another of a child struggling to hold an iguana, are described by the artist as “exploring our relationship with the natural world.”

Also on show in the Cop Green Zone and an especially jarring symbol of the deep schisms and incompatible agendas that characterised this latest Conference of the Parties were five animal sculptures created from discarded electronic and industrial defence waste materials. These were part of the “Upcycling a Future Vision” art collection launched by Aselsan, Turkey’s largest defence contractor to demonstrate its “commitment to a circular economy”, according to Turkish state-run media, as well as to celebrate the company’s 50th anniversary and “future of more efficient, innovative and sustainable production.” In a further irony, the defence giant—which is majority owned by the Turkish Armed Forces Foundation and produces electronic warfare technology and naval and air defence missile systems—was awarded a Green Transformation certificate from the Turkish authorities in tribute to its sustainability efforts. These apparently include a five-year road map to maximise energy, water and raw material efficiency whilst reducing carbon emissions and recycling 87% of total waste.

But amidst the chaos and anomalies within Cop some consolation can be gleaned from the fact that, while the oil-producing countries united to derail proceedings (undoubtedly spurred by the absence of an official US delegation and the Trump administration's overt hostility to the global fight to combat climate change), nonetheless 193 countries plus the EU remain committed to the Paris Agreement. Collectively these nations account for around 85% of global emissions. And while not wrapped up in a final deal, a number of significant agreements were made at Cop31 which included countries backing faster electrification and clean energy, drawing up measures to cut methane emissions and passing measures to protect the planet’s forests and oceans and strengthen support for communities impacted by climate change.

Beyond the Cop negotiating rooms, there are also glimmers of progress. In the UK greenhouse gas emissions have fallen by more than 50% since 1990 (although this much-vaunted statistic doesn’t include international aviation, shipping and imports and exports, which makes it more like 24%, according to the Office for National Statistics). Solar panels now provide 28% of Pakistan’s power while France and Denmark have announced roadmaps to phase out all fossil fuel by 2050, with Spain, Portugal and other countries planning to do the same. While these shifts often have as much to do with the fall in the cost of renewable technology and its resilience to market swings as a desire to hit climate goals; nonetheless an incremental frustration at the Cop consensus model means that countries are increasingly going it alone in naming what needs to be done and in identifying how they will tackle it.

Still from The People's Emergency Briefing (2026) featuring naturalist and presenter Chris Packham

Case in point was last Monday (16 November) when, as Cop31 was rumbling on, an important milestone was reached in the UK as Parliament debated a nearly 139,000 strong petition which called for the government to hold a UK-wide emergency briefing on the climate and nature crisis. The petition had been generated by the National Emergency Briefing (NEB), a public information campaign consisting of an influential group of leading experts and fronted by the British naturalist and BBC TV presenter Chris Packham. It was asking for a “prime-time Covid-style briefing across all channels” which would be introduced by the Prime Minister and delivered by independent experts in order to spell out the extent and risks posed by climate change and nature loss, along with the action—both public and governmental—that needs to be taken. More than seventy members of parliament from across the political spectrum attended the three-hour debate which ended broadly in favour of the proposed televised emergency briefing, although not officially agreed. Speaking for the government, climate transition minister Katie White MP did go on record to state that she and her colleagues would meet with the leaders of the NEB campaign and “explore opportunities to work together”, and work on public engagement within the government's climate and nature security taskforce.

Just as Westminster was being galvanised by the NEB campaign, so too was the art world. Two days after the briefing debate, Tate Modern hosted a packed screening of The People’s Emergency Briefing, a 50-minute documentary film made by the NEB and presented by Packham. An articulate panel of nine experts starkly presented the urgent threats that climate and nature breakdown pose to food security, nature, the economy, national security and public health. This film, which anyone can freely register to screen, has been responsible for fueling much of the groundswell of both public and parliamentary support for the NEB’s petition. Since its release in April last year, The People’s Emergency Briefing has been shown more than 5000 times across myriad sectors and in venues large and small throughout the UK, from church halls, offices and hospitals, with many more scheduled for the forthcoming months. As Katie White declared at the Parliamentary debate, “a film has become a movement.”

However—with a few notable exceptions—the People’s Emergency Briefing has not had much airing in the art world. But now this seems set to change thanks to the art world environmental charity the Gallery Climate Coalition (GCC), who organised the screening and the following panel discussion. This was chaired by Frances Morris, the former director of Tate Modern and nowthe GCC's chair, speaking with artist Heather Ackroyd and Peter Lefort, the green futures network manager at the University of Exeter.

The screening of The People's Emergency Briefing at Tate Modern on 18 November 2026

Among the two-hundred strong audience of artists, including Cornelia Parker and Marcus Coates, academics and art workers from across both the public and commercial sectors, there emerged a strong determination to galvanise action. Many declared a commitment to lobby their MPs, to organise screenings of the People’s Emergency Briefing in their galleries and generally to be more courageous in both acting individually and collectively to help instigate what Peter Lefort compellingly described as “positive tipping points.”

As Lefort explained, these tipping points occur when cumulative changes in behaviour, policies, expectations and attitudes reinforce each other and gather momentum to accelerate change and achieve transformative impact. As politicians falter and our systems for joining forces globally become increasingly dysfunctional and inflexible, it now seems increasingly clear that these new forces for change—such as the NEB, with allied activist groups and screenings occuring across Europe—are coming from the grassroots up, and that the creativity of the art world needs to be applied to shift ossified, seemingly intractable structures and open up new ways of thinking.

After all, it was back in 2019 that, on the instigation of artist duo Heather Ackroyd and Dan Harvey, a procession of bell ringing artworkers headed by a woman wearing a coat of living grass and riding a white horse, occupied Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall. The event from the Culture Declares Emergency movement inspired then-director Frances Morris to make the institution of Tate declare a climate and ecological emergency, helping set in motion an increased environmental awareness that is now common currency throughout the art world. In the words of one attendee at last week’s Tate Modern gathering, “we may be small compared to other sectors but we can be LOUD!” So now let’s brush ourselves down after Cop and make our voices heard, before it is too late.

Partners of the organisation are now rewarded for adhering to its decarbonising and emission-cutting guidelines

#9058. Five key projects by Dezeen Awards emerging architect of the year Kuma&Elsa

This year Kuma&Elsa was named emerging architect of the year at the Dezeen Awards. Here, they select five projects that demonstrate the ethos of the studio.

Led by Japanese architect Shohei Kuma and French-Spanish urban designer Elsa Escobedo, Kuma&Elsa has completed a wide variety of projects from their bases in France and Japan.

“We believe it is important not to impose a common consistency across our projects,” Kuma told Dezeen.

“Every project is unique, shaped by a one-off combination of site and client. Preserving that uniqueness requires an open mind. Personally, I quickly lose interest when things are planned in advance.”

“That said, there are certain topics, many of which are shared by our generation, such as feminism, the care for natural resources and a shared public space, that interest us on a personal level, and I imagine they find their way into our work,” added Escobedo.

“We try to approach them with a sense of joy.”

Although they have already designed a wide range of projects, from installations to houses and public toilets, the duo would like to work on more varied schemes and unusual projects, along with completing their own, long-running renovation.

“It would be nice to actually finish this self-renovation project at some point…” said Escobedo.

“More seriously, I’d love to experiment with the reuse of materials on a larger scale, or in a European context, working with European craftspeople.”

“I would love to work on overlooked building types and uses, especially those that have little place in architectural history and attract few expectations,” added Kuma. “Designing a toilet pavilion for the Expo, a building type that nobody expects to become architecture, is one example.”

Along with the variety in projects, both architects agreed that the wide range of daily activities is what they most enjoy about being an architect.

“The variety, the diversity,” said Escobedo, when asked about her favourite part about being an architect.

“One day you’re on a construction site with incredible Japanese carpenters, the next you’re discussing a detail with your favourite thermal engineer, the following week you’re taking part in a conversation with colleagues you admire, before finding yourself struggling to install the plumbing and tiles in a shower because you had the brilliant idea of taking on a self-build project.”

Kuma also added that he enjoys the intensity of working on site.

“The construction site,” he said. “Nothing is more stressful or demanding, with all the struggles involving people and money. Yet every time I see a building taking shape, I feel glad I chose architecture. There is something addictive about it.”

Read on to find out five key projects by Dezeen Award-winning studio Kuma&Elsa, as described by the duo:

“The client’s childhood home, a traditional Japanese house, has an engawa gallery open to the garden. The new residence occupies the top two floors of a building owned by the client. She, along with her two sons and their families, will move into three apartments located on the sixth and seventh floors.

“At the centre of each apartment, we inserted a hut-like volume that gathers the quieter rooms: a small living room and the bedrooms. In the space carved out around it emerges an intermediate zone – an engawa that serves both as a place to stay and as a passage.

“Balcony, engawa, and hut thus form three spatial layers that resonate with the childhood home. The structure consists of Y-shaped modules made of lightweight steel sections and bracing cables, typically used in shelving systems.

“These modules are arranged two by two in mirrored pairs along a regular grid, with occasional inversions. From these new dwellings, one can look down across the street at the engawa of the childhood home. This project does not seek to nostalgically replicate that memory-laden place, but rather to build a new home nourished by the memories of the old one.”

“One water is a bathing and rest pavilion for the Osaka World Expo 2025. Toilets are at first glance a pragmatic facility, dedicated to human physiology. But they are also intimately linked to contemporary issues such as the use of natural resources and gender.

“One water uses the path of rainfall on the accessible roof and its subsequent accumulation to create encounters between water and the public, and contribute to the supply of the toilets.

“The design of the pavilion allows for the reuse of materials and structural components, and makes no gender distinction in the toilets, because, after all, ‘we are all fish in one water’.”

House by the temple, Saitama Prefecture, Japan, 2024

“The house is opposite the entrance of a temple that is surrounded by a park of ancient trees and a wall, as if it belongs to another world. Reflecting this closed composition, we designed the house as an everyday world for a family.

“The main building is located at the back of the plot and has a quarter-circle plan to reduce its own shadow. The street facade is a single-storey hut, which creates a continuity between the open space of the park and the garden of the house.

“On the ground floor, the park is the backdrop to the house. On the first floor, each room offers distant views of the temple, like an observatory.”

“A daily public space in a residential area. We create a plaza in a small residential area where human life is still at human scale.

“The house is like the background that forms the square. The composition consists of various couples: the smooth black mortar of the outer wall and the rough crushed black basalt ground, the emerald entrance hut and the crape myrtle tree with white flowers, the interior spaces and the outside square.”

Water Flower Courtyard, Montpellier, France, 2019

“The life of a flower is short: we wanted to express the fragility of a concentrated life from flowering to dispersal. This project was open to the public for a week during the Montpellier architecture festival Festival des Architectures Vives in June 2019.

“Eighteen lightweight units made of two-millimetre-thick aluminium sheets are laid out together as a forest.

“The tube is a vase that contains water and peony flowers, the bowl contains water and slate stones. All structures are self-supporting and their stability works as in a roly-poly toy. After a few days, petals start falling on the surface of the water.”

We'll also be sharing tips and tricks, reviews and guides to help you find your perfect iPad match, whether you're a digital artist or an everyday commuter after a lightweight workhorse tablet. And if Apple gear is your thing, our Apple Black Friday deals hub has even more to browse.

Looking for a tablet that covers the essentials, whether that's browsing, streaming box sets, sketching or taking notes? Apple's standard iPad is still a smart buy. It debuted in March 2025 at $349, before Apple lifted the price to $449 in July 2026 as part of a lineup-wide increase. This offer is the cheapest we've seen it since that happened.

Apple's M4 iPad Air only arrived in March, which makes this $100 cut a strong contender for the best Black Friday deal on it. We'd point most buyers here: it costs well under the Pro, yet it supports the Apple Pencil Pro and packs enough muscle for digital painting, photo retouching and the odd Final Cut edit. If you'd like a bigger canvas, the 13-inch version has also dropped by $100.

This is a solid but fairly run-of-the-mill saving on the base 11-inch iPad Pro. The bigger deal is at B&H, where the 13-inch Pro, which earned 4.5 stars from us, is $100 cheaper, and opting for the 512GB model lifts your saving to as much as $150.

If you're after something that can genuinely stand in for a laptop, this tablet is up to the job, with ample power for demanding graphics work and video editing. Its OLED display reaches a peak brightness of 1600 nits for HDR content, and the smooth 120Hz refresh rate keeps everything feeling responsive.

Apple's newest iPad mini only landed earlier this month, so a discount this good, this soon, caught us off guard. Our design editor put it through its paces a couple of weeks back and came away impressed by the new OLED screen (no other iPad outside the Pro line has one), the quicker A20 Pro chip and the better speakers. Apple Pencil Pro support is still on board as well.

Happy to settle for last generation's 2024 model with the A17 Pro chip and a non-OLED display? Amazon has it marked down to $499.

Another accessory that can unlock an iPad's true potential, especially an iPad Pros, is a good portable SSD drive.

With the standard iPad, you're limited to a max of 512GB internal storage. With the iPad Pros, you can choose up to 2TB. That is a lot of storage space for a tablet, but a 2TB iPad Pro is expensive, and if you're using it as a laptop standing for thinks like editing high-resolution video footage or working on large design projects, it's going to fill up anyway, unless you're working largely in the cloud.

A portable SSD helps you back everything up quickly, you can work directly off the external drive if it's fast enough, and it has more flexibility than internal storage since you can plug it into another device whenever you want.

#9056. Argentina leads the way in repatriating Indigenous human remains, study says

The director of the Australian Museum, Kim McKay, and Koro Johnny Tuki, representing the Rapa Nui people, mark the handing over of remains of Indigenous people in July Photo: Louise Reily; © Australian Museum

Driven largely by Indigenous activism, the repatriation of ancestral human remains in Chile and Argentina is pushing museums, universities and scientific institutions to re-examine longstanding practices of collection, research and display. A recent study by the Chilean researchers Jacinta Arthur and Patricia Ayala suggests that the movement has opened a crucial ethical debate in both countries, with key differences: while Chile has handled repatriation campaigns on a case-by-case basis, Argentina has emerged as a regional leader since passing a law specifically tackling the issue.

“Argentina is central to any discussion of this issue in South America, since it is the first country in the region with a law specifically aimed at the restitution of Indigenous human remains,” Ayala, an archaeologist at the Universidad de Chile, Santiago tells The Art Newspaper. “In Chile, by contrast, there is no legal framework of this kind. That is why it was both necessary and interesting to compare the two realities.”

The researchers’ article, “Indigenous Repatriation Movements in South America and Their Repercussions on Ethical Discussions on the Respectful Treatment of Human Remains: The Cases of Chile and Argentina”, was published on 11 September in the journal Latin American Antiquity. It emerged from Arthur and Ayala’s work with Indigenous communities in Chile, particularly the campaigns led by the Atacameño and Rapa Nui people, where demands for the respectful treatment of human remains include critiques of their scientific study, museum display, sample collection, repatriation and reburial.

Those efforts were underscored last July, when the Australian Museum in Sydney returned the remains of ancestors of the Rapa Nui people who had been removed from sacred burial sites at Rano Raraku during a German naval expedition in 1882, and acquired by the museum the following year. The institution’s director, Kim McKay, publicly acknowledged the circumstances under which the ancestors’ remains had entered the collection, and said: “Returning them is an act of moral responsibility.”

According to Ayala, despite the legal differences between Argentina and Chile, the treatment of human remains from an Indigenous perspective “has not yet become central to scientific concerns”. Indigenous activism, she says, has forced museums and archaeologists to confront “the exclusion of Indigenous voices” and “alternative knowledge and ontologies” linked to ancestral bodies and the materials associated with them. It has also brought renewed attention to the violence of looting, collecting and scientific research that helped shape colonial and national museums, where Indigenous ancestral remains have ended up since at least the 19th century.

“In this context, both museums and academic fields have begun to reflect on their practices and discourses,” Ayala says, “although much work remains to be done to fully integrate the rights of Indigenous peoples in both countries.”

Argentina passed a law in 2001 mandating that Indigenous human remains held in public or private collections must be made available to the peoples or communities that claim them. An implementing decree followed in 2010, making the National Institute of Indigenous Affairs responsible for surveying and identifying remains, and coordinating their return.

A recent case at the Museo Etnográfico Juan B. Ambrosetti, part of the Universidad de Buenos Aires, shows how such restitutions unfold in practice. Last May the museum returned the remains of an Inca child from Apu Chañi, along with his grave goods, to El Angosto and Sol de Mayo, two communities in the El Moreno area of Jujuy state. The child had entered the museum’s collection in 1905, after being brought down from a hill on Nevado de Chañi. Following the restitution, a mausoleum was built at the foot of the mountain to display the grave goods, while the child’s remains will be buried at high altitude when conditions in the freezing high Andes allow.

“What I think is missing here, above all, is getting ahead of restitutions, not waiting for communities to file a claim,” Andrea Pegoraro, the director of the Museo Etnográfico, tells The Art Newspaper. Pegoraro, says the return of the child from Apu Chañi shows that Argentina has a more developed legal framework than many neighbouring countries, but also exposes the limits of a policy based solely on responding to claims.

That, she says, is one of the challenges still facing Argentine museums: moving from responding to specific requests to actively reviewing collections, identifying provenance gaps, reconstructing acquisition histories and contacting the relevant communities. In the Apu Chañi case, she says, the museum reviewed archival and archaeological records to establish where the remains had been taken and to which community they should be returned.

At the restitution ceremony, Pegoraro said the museum was not handing over “a heritage object or an object of study”, but rather “an ancestor to his territory and his people”. The community, in turn, described the returned ancestor as “a guardian” connected to water and life in the Puna region of Jujuy.

For Pegoraro, the distinction between human remains and objects is crucial. “If they are human remains, I am fully in favour of returning them, and the community must decide what to do with them,” she says. Objects raise a different set of considerations, in her view: to whom they should be returned, what happens to them and how museums can ensure access for other communities.

Reconstructing provenance is essential to any restitution process, Pegoraro adds, because Indigenous territories do not always align with today’s political boundaries. “Communities inhabit territories that did not previously have the political or geographical boundaries we have today,” she says. Museums often rely on documentation archaeologists wrote at the time the remains entered a collection, even when the places they recorded no longer correspond neatly to current jurisdictions.

Pegoraro also warns that change cannot be limited to isolated restitutions. “The integration of Indigenous communities does not come only through rhetoric, or by carrying out a restitution or holding an exhibition once in a while, but by literally working side by side,” she says. She adds that collaboration must include the ongoing rewriting of exhibition narratives, as well as financial compensation.

In Pegoraro’s view, the current movement for repatriation of Indigenous remains and artefacts began in the 1980s, especially in the US, Australia, New Zealand and Canada. In Argentina and elsewhere in South America, she adds, those demands gained force with the return of democracy after dictatorships. In Europe, however, museums carry “a much stronger colonial history”, she says, and while some countries are beginning to talk about decolonising collections, returning objects or rewriting narratives, “they still have a long way to go. It must not remain just rhetoric.”

The restituted human remains include 17 skulls and one sample of hair, which were taken from the island during a German expedition in 1882

On public view for the first time, the objects were all returned during outgoing president Gustavo Petro’s administration

The institution intensified its repatriation efforts after revised federal rules governing Native American remains and funerary objects went into effect earlier this year

#9054. Biscuit-tin lids, horse brasses and scrap metal form sculptural V&A Christmas tree by Burberry

Fashion brand Burberry‘s chief creative officer Daniel Lee worked with artist Ann Carrington to create a Christmas tree sculpture for the Victoria & Albert Museum, made from “memories, traditions and little treasures.”

The 16-foot (4.8-metre) tree, which was unveiled this week, sits in the entrance hall of the Victoria & Albert Museum (VA’s) South Kensington location and was designed to celebrate craft and creativity.

“This collaboration with Ann is a celebration of creativity and what better place to showcase this than the V&A?” Lee said. “It’s one of my favourite museums and a constant source of inspiration to me.”

Lee and Carrington made the tree from old money boxes, biscuit and sweet-tin lids, trinket dishes, silver trays, horse brasses and embossed plates, which were turned into rosettes and ribbons and attached to a metal frame.

The tree, which was made as part of Burberry‘s 170th anniversary celebrations, also features ribbons and bows made of scrap metal.

According to Lee, he and Carrington made the sculpture from “memories, traditions and little treasures. Objects and materials that most people would overlook.”

Carrington added that the design was inspired by the ritual of getting old Christmas decorations out of storage in time for the festive season.

“We wanted to capture that magical moment when you retrieve the battered old box of Christmas decorations from the loft, sift through the faded party bows and tattered tinsel accumulated through the generations and begin the joyful ritual of dressing the tree,” she said.

“I’m always drawn to work that’s handmade, and Ann is a master of her craft,” Lee said of the collaboration.

As well as the tree, the V&A will also be showing The Burberry Trench: Crafting an Icon, a display that traces the history of the trench coat. Burberry has a multi-year partnership with the museum and is set to open The Burberry Gallery at the South Kensington location in 2028.

Lee has previously unveiled an archive-inspired logo for Burberry, and a few years ago, the brand revealed its redesigned London flagship store.

Wunder Werkz mixes architectural heritage with playful design.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Denver Design District has unveiled a slick new brand identity, transforming the once exclusive design commerce hub into a fresh cultural destination. A blend of design-focused goods, art, retail and food, the new identity marks a more accessible, culturally relevant district made for the masses.

While there's no formula for creating the best rebrands, Denver Design District's new identity shines in its attention to detail, honouring its rich design heritage while embracing a newfound playfulness. Sleek, timeless and characterful, the new brand identity is the ultimate love letter to design.

Created in collaboration with D4 Urban and design studio Wunder Werkz, the Denver Design District rebrand centres around a wonderfully contemporary brandmark. Representing the district's evolution, the 3 'Ds' motif compresses the bold letterforms by a third each time, making for a dynamic visual anchor.

To accomodate the brandmark, Wunder Werkz created DDD Standard, a bespoke midweight sans serif, to act as the district's display typeface. Equal parts "architectural and playful", it draws inspiration from Herbert Bayer's mid-century furniture forms. Paired with an iconographic system of silhouetted design products, clarity and cohesion flow throughout the identity with a confident authority.

“The idea was to make a more welcoming, accessible district; one that celebrates design in all its forms,” explains Jon Hartman, Partner at Wunder Werkz. “Trade remains an important part of the ecosystem, but it is no longer the whole story. So, we needed to design a brand that felt open and culturally relevant while still carrying the credibility of the design industry.”

A rich colour system of brick, blush, slate and deep yellow contrasts the tans and greys of the district's buildings, bringing warmth and personality to the clean design. The result is a refined homage to design that feels accessible and unpretentious, without losing the slick essence of the design district.

“This project represents the kind of work we love most because it allows us to engage at every level, from strategy and stakeholder alignment through implementation and installation,” adds Hartman. “For us, that’s where the best work happens. Not when design is treated as an afterthought, but when it becomes the link between strategy, space and experience. The result is a brand that feels cohesive at every scale, from a website headline to a warehouse-sized building facade.”

A will (technically a "last will and testament") is a legal document that specifies how your assets should be distributed after your death. It must go through probate — a court-supervised process that validates the will, pays debts and taxes, and distributes assets to beneficiaries. A living trust (specifically a revocable living trust) is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. When you die, the successor trustee distributes those assets according to the trust terms — without court involvement.

You need both: A trust does not name guardians for minor children (only a will can do that), and a trust only controls assets that have been formally transferred into it. A pour-over will acts as a safety net — it directs any assets not in the trust at your death to pour into the trust, where they are distributed according to the trust terms. The pour-over will still goes through probate, but it ensures nothing falls through the cracks.

The term "living trust" almost always refers to a revocable living trust — one you can change, amend, or dissolve at any time during your lifetime. You remain the trustee, manage the assets as you always have, and pay taxes on trust income using your personal Social Security number. For income tax purposes, a revocable trust is invisible — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist.

An irrevocable trust is fundamentally different. Once established, you cannot easily modify it, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. This permanence provides two powerful advantages:

The federal estate tax exemption is $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples) in 2026, but this historically high exemption is scheduled to sunset after 2025, potentially dropping to approximately $7 million per person. FIRE households who have built $3 million to $10 million in net worth through decades of saving and investment growth should monitor this sunset closely. If the exemption drops, irrevocable trusts become relevant at much lower wealth levels.

For most FIRE households with $1 million to $5 million in net worth, a revocable living trust provides the right balance of control, flexibility, and probate avoidance. Irrevocable structures become compelling only when estate tax exposure is real or asset protection needs are elevated.

Estate planning is governed primarily by state law, and the value of a living trust versus a will varies significantly depending on where you live.

Nine states are community property states: Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington, and Wisconsin. In these states, most assets acquired during marriage are owned 50/50 by both spouses regardless of whose name is on the title. At death, only the deceased spouse's half passes through their estate plan.

The remaining 41 states follow common law (also called "equitable distribution"). Ownership depends on whose name is on the title. This distinction affects how assets pass at death and whether a trust or will provides better spousal protection.

Use this framework to determine whether you need a trust, a will, or both:

A revocable living trust is strongly recommended if:

Remember that a trust only controls assets titled in the trust's name. After creating a trust, you must fund it by re-titling your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust. Unfunded trusts — trusts that exist on paper but hold no assets — provide zero benefit. The pour-over will catches stragglers, but relying entirely on the pour-over defeats the purpose because those assets still go through probate.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The most common estate planning mistake with trusts is failing to fund them. Creating a trust document costs $1,500 to $5,000, but if you never transfer your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust, it provides zero probate avoidance. After signing your trust, immediately re-title assets into the trust name. Your attorney should provide a funding checklist. An unfunded trust sitting in a drawer is an expensive piece of paper — not an estate plan.

Yes. A pour-over will catches any assets not transferred into your trust during your lifetime and directs them into the trust at death. A will is also the only legal document that can name guardians for minor children. Every trust-based estate plan should include a pour-over will.

A revocable living trust prepared by an estate planning attorney typically costs $1,500 to $5,000, depending on complexity and your location. This usually includes the trust document, pour-over will, powers of attorney, healthcare directives, and initial funding guidance. Online trust services cost $200 to $500 but may not address state-specific issues or complex situations.

Yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as both the grantor (creator) and the trustee (manager). You maintain full control over all trust assets during your lifetime. You name a successor trustee who takes over only if you become incapacitated or die.

A revocable living trust does not reduce estate taxes — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist for income and estate tax purposes. However, a trust can be structured with provisions (such as an A/B trust or disclaimer trust) that maximize the use of both spouses' estate tax exemptions. For estate tax reduction, irrevocable trusts are the primary tool.

A revocable trust can be changed, amended, or dissolved at any time. You maintain full control. An irrevocable trust generally cannot be changed after creation, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. Revocable trusts provide probate avoidance and incapacity planning. Irrevocable trusts provide estate tax reduction and asset protection.

Without a trust, each state where you own real property requires a separate probate proceeding (called ancillary probate), multiplying costs and complexity. Transferring out-of-state property into a living trust eliminates ancillary probate entirely — the successor trustee can transfer or sell the property without court involvement in any state.

#9051. After nearly two decades, the Old Acropolis Museum in Athens re-opens

Michael Rakowitz, What You Leave Behind Is Not What Is Engraved (2026)

Courtesy the artist and Neon. Commissioned by Neon. © Natalia Tsoukala

The Old Acropolis Museum, the first Greek museum to be built in modern times, re-opened on Monday after a major restoration project. It is the first time the museum, founded in 1874 and nestled into the rock of the storied Acropolis hill, has been accessible to the public since 2007.

The opening ceremony was a grand affair, with speeches by the Greek prime minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and the country’s minister of culture Lina Mendoni, among others.

Once simply the “Museum”, the Old Acropolis Museum took its current name in 2009, when Athens built a newer Acropolis Museum 300 yards down the hill. This offered larger and state-of-the-art space in which to house the antiquities from the Parthenon and other Greek sites, as well as a viewing room designed for the Elgin Marbles—currently showing casts, but with the idea that one day the museum might one day welcome the real items.

The Old Acropolis Museum was left empty for years, and plans eventually developed to use it as storage and administrative spaces. But by 2019, the Greek state definitively nixed this idea.

“For us, it was inconceivable, almost an affront, that this historic building, with its unique location, should be converted into offices and storage facilities,” said Mendoni during her opening speech. “We therefore decided that the museum should reopen in accordance with its original purpose. However, it was not to become just another conventional museum, but rather a museum and exhibition space hosting exhibitions on the history, archaeology and culture of Athens, as well as contemporary art exhibitions inspired by Greek civilisation and innovative programmes incorporating cutting-edge technology.”

The museum will now host both a rotating selection of artefacts as well as a contemporary art programme. The first exhibition, Athens City Idea, focuses on Athens as a social, political, and economic entity, via tragic masks, statues, coins, and amphorae that have been in storage elsewhere across Athens, plus recent discoveries. A digital art component animated the Parthenon’s friezes and the history of the Acropolis Hill.

Part of the idea behind the temporary exhibitions is to keep the museum’s display current, a point also underlined by its commitment to contemporary art.

This includes the last of a trilogy of works commissioned for Athens from the American artist Michael Rakowitz, which is also the final project of Neon, the roving art foundation created by Dimitris Daskalopoulos that for 14 years has funded art and exhibitions across the city, and which announced its closure earlier this year.

“You could say that the first contemporary work here was Phidias’s statue of Athena in the 5th century BCE,” quipped Daskalopoulos, the Athens-born collector who founded Neon. Daskalopoulos also supported the refurbishment of the Old Acropolis Museum, which was funded by both private and public money. “But encouraging the coexistence of antiquity with the contemporary is a challenge we have embraced many times throughout our work at Neon.”

Michael Rakowitz and Elina Kountouri, the director of Neon, outside the reopened Old Acropolis Museum

Rakowitz’s installation What You Leave Behind Is Not What Is Engraved (2026), which was commissioned by Neon, and comprises a kiln and newly fired bricks, looks at a lesser-known episode in the Acropolis’s history.

“I realised that you could only tell the whole story of the site if you look through the lens of migration,” the artist told The Art Newspaper. He studied the population exchanges during the collapse of the Ottoman Empire, when Greece and Turkey forced a combined total of around 1.5 million inhabitants to leave—Christian Turks to Greece and Muslim Greeks to Turkey. When the Turkish refugees arrived in Athens, they set up tents and encampments at the base of the Acropolis hill.

“Thinking about a ruin as being something that can renew itself to a population and become once again a shelter excited me,” he said. "When I found out about the tradition of the Asia Minor refugees who were able to go back to Turkey after some years, and then the Muslims who were uprooted from Greece, when those populations were able to visit their the departed homelands, they found oftentimes their buildings or towns in a state of ruin, and they would take a brick from that place and bring it back as a memento.”

Installation view of Michael Rakowitz, What You Leave Behind Is Not What Is Engraved (2026)

Courtesy the artist and Neon. Commissioned by Neon. © Natalia Tsoukala

Rakowitz has incorporated these original bricks alongside ones newly made with inscriptions and stamps that bear witness to more recent histories of displacement. For these he worked with survivors of the 1920s population transfers as well as women in the Melissa Network, a nonprofit organisation that supports migrant women in Greece.

“I wanted these bricks to become a foundation for a new kind of city that welcomes strangers and doesn't push them back at sea,” he said.

After sponsoring many exhibitions and commissions across his native Greece, Neon founder Dimitris Daskalopoulos will continue to fund individual projects in Athens and several curatorial posts

Pandermalis, a revered archaeologist and professor, had also been outspoken in calling for the reunification of all the Parthenon marbles in Athens

Athens are still hopeful that the marbles will be returned, to be be housed in the currently unfinished New Acropolis Museum

The Acropolis museum is under construction, and the design for the permanent exhibition is in preparation

#9050. Meet Courage Dzidula Kpodo, Lesley Lokko's pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

Photography by Cyril Marcilhacy. unless stated

Ghanaian-Scottish architect Lesley Lokko has nominated Courage Dzidula Kpodo as a key name to watch over the next two decades for Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler.

In this interview he explains why despite growing global attention, his ambitions remain resolutely local.

Having only graduated in 2025 from a master’s in architecture at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) – for which he was awarded the Arthur Rotch Prize for highest overall mark – Kpodo is already someone Lokko believes will “help shape the next chapter of African architecture”.

Kpodo’s work, which sees him blur the roles of architect, artist and archivist, is focused on revealing what he calls the “silences” in prevailing narratives about Ghanaian architecture, and challenging the idea that Ghana’s future development must be a “linear prescription of urbanisation”.

If this sounds theoretical or speculative, Kpodo’s approach is anything but: the site of his MIT thesis was an almost five-acre stretch of farmland in Ghana to which he purchased a 99-year lease in 2022, and is currently using as a live site to consider alternative forms of development in the region.

Stating how, if nothing else, the purchase would “preserve the value of the money I had in my savings account,” Kpodo sees the site becoming an alternative institution of sorts, constructed using materials he has salvaged from vernacular buildings that would otherwise be demolished.

“The committee at MIT was a bit shocked, because they weren’t used to the idea of a thesis project existing in the real world,” Kpodo told Dezeen. “But I still thought of it as almost as a sort of sketch, just at 1:1 scale.”

“Doing that gives you something to test – people are going to interface with it; you can test out its failures and success very quickly.”

Growing up in Kumasi, Kpodo initially focused on visual art in school before pursuing a course in architecture at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), and subsequently MIT.

At KNUST he was quickly exposed to narratives around both architectural success and Ghana’s own architectural history that left him seeking something more “homegrown”.

“We had a lecture from Francis Kéré in which he spoke about his Serpentine Pavilion, and how taking on commissions from big institutions or big clients can become critical for defining your practice,” said Kpodo.

I thought: okay, what can I do now that is within my means instead of waiting for the big commissions to come?

“At the time, I couldn’t imagine any of these commissions coming to those of us working in the South. I couldn’t see any architects who were operating on that scale, or even at a kind of global scale,” he continued.

“It almost had the opposite effect on me. I thought: okay, what can I do now that is within my means instead of waiting for the big commissions to come? I think it’s by being local that I can have something to offer to the world.”

Kpodo became interested in local architectural archives, initially those of the KNUST Development Office, but also the less formalised collections of images and drawings that he encountered online.

He soon helped establish Postbox Ghana, a research collective initiated by artist Manuela Nebuloni to create an alternative architectural archive using postcards and stamps from the 1950s to the 1980s, which often depicted examples of Tropical Modernism and state infrastructure constructed following Ghana’s independence.

However, Kpodo still felt that these archival materials did not speak to his own understanding of Ghanaian architecture, having grown up in a “not-so-well-to-do context” in Kumasi and only really encountering modernist architecture when first entering the KNUST campus.

“The whole archive that I was exposed to, whether it was in the Development Office or in the postcards, had a huge, significant gap in it,” he said. “I remember stories my dad would tell me about building practices and cultures that just didn’t make it into this archive or our training in architecture school.”

“As a newly independent country, Ghana wanted to break away from any kind of ethnographic notion of what the ‘Gold Coast’ – to use its colonial name – was. So those ‘traditional’ buildings and other forms of practices did not make it into the framework of thinking about what our future meant,” he continued.

“But even though these buildings are far removed from the city centres and from the archive, they were foundational in the sense that they enabled the cocoa industry, and brought in the money that built the institutions and structures that are enshrined in postcards.”

Kpodo began to photograph these vernacular buildings himself, many of them farm structures made using laterite, a type of local red earth that is formed into air and sun-dried blocks for construction

When I talk about rebuilding them, it usually lands. People get it, and then they begin asking, ‘okay, but what can it be?’

Upon finding many of these buildings slated for demolition, Kpodo has more recently begun to purchase them, before carefully deconstructing their laterite structures to become the raw material for new structures on his land.

The idea was initially met locally with some confusion. “I remember one man said, ‘oh, are you going to extract gold from the walls?’ because laterite can contain gold,” he recalled.

“But when I talk about rebuilding them, it usually lands. People get it, and then they begin asking, ‘okay, but what can it be?’ And then some kids would even begin making their own proposals. For me, just creating that imagination is worth it.”

The land that Kpodo purchased in 2022 is in Ghana’s eastern region, and was at the frontier of cocoa production in the early 1900s. Some descendants of the first farmers on the land are still based there, and were among those Kpodo interviewed to understand the history of the landscape.

Alongside the widening of a communal path – the focus of his MIT thesis – and the moving of vernacular building materials there, he has also constructed a simple timber deck, both as a rest point for the farmers and an observation point for watching future changes unfold on the site.

If I were asked to design a Serpentine Pavilion, I’d probably make a replica in Ghana, too. You can only do so much in an exhibition setting

Kpodo envisions that this future will include both new agricultural processing facilities for the farmers on the land, as well as community spaces that enable further discussions around its ongoing development.

This work also forms the basis of Kpodo’s educational and curatorial work. He is keen to continue “speaking both languages” – the more practical with the conceptual – but he feels the latter should always be grounded in a “local base” rather than detached from it.

In 2023, his work with Postbox Ghana was exhibited at both Vantage Point Sharjah and the Venice Architecture Biennale. In 2025, he curated the LagosPhoto Biennial alongside Maria Pia Bernardoni and Robin Beth Riskin, with the theme of Incarceration.

Kpodo also taught on the one-month Nomadic African Studio at the African Futures Institute, founded by Lokko as a space “dedicated to rethinking education, culture, and practice from the African continent outward.”

Most recently, he orchestrated the transportation of the wall of a laterite farmhouse a little further afield to the Fondation Cartier in Paris, as part of the exhibition Ibrahim Mahama: Harvest Season, where it is accompanied by images from the Postbox Ghana archives.

“If I were asked to design a Serpentine Pavilion, I’d probably make a replica in Ghana, too,” he said. “You can only do so much in an exhibition setting. You can only talk so much. If the work has no ground and no local base, then I think it becomes very difficult for you to bridge what it is that you’re presenting versus the work that it proposes to be doing.”

“We need to cultivate other sites that do the real work, sites that translate it into something which is not necessarily concerned with an educated audience,” he continued.

“My sense is that we’re increasingly going to see the most ‘powerful’ institutions seek out these hyper-local narratives and projects as a way to really understand the world.”

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews. The series is presented in partnership with Kohler.

#9049. Anxiety Tattoos: How Ink Therapy Can Help Ease Mental Health Struggles

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry. For some peeps, they’re the go-to for commemorating life wins or solidifying deep-seated beliefs — from quotes that got you through dark times or portraits of your fave pets.

The act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience. The machine’s buzz and the needle’s sharp sting are part of a ritual that may help bring internal battles to the surface. But is there a link between anxiety and the decision to get tatted? Could framing your fears and anxieties in gorgeous designs help you cope? Continue reading to find out.

For many, tattoos are much more than art. Peeps who have anxiety may get tattoos as a way of taking control over their narrative, including their mental health struggles.

Anxiety disorder makes life challenging, and you may feel you’re stuck in a rip tide of continual worry, fear, and dread. Even if you know it’s the anxiety talking, you can still struggle to contain these overwhelming feelings, and it’s exhausting. Anxiety can trick your mind, tell you you’re unworthy, and there’s no way out.

But here’s where tattoos come into play — they create a visual shoutout to your strength and resilience. Imagine marking your skin with reminders of the battles you’ve won and what you’ve overcome.

Getting inked can feel like grabbing the reins back from anxiety and stress. A tattoo is an affirmation. It can turn your invisible battle scars into something tangible and beautiful, giving a sense of ownership over your body and experiences. This is huge when anxiety tries to convince you that you don’t have a say in your own story.

Whether it’s a poignant quote, a symbolic image, or just a badass design, a tattoo packs a punch of personal significance and your enduring strength. You’ve taken a deliberate, proactive step to help you take greater control over your life, and that should be celebrated.

Psychologically, tattoos are visual high-fives to yourself. For the anxious folks, tats are a way to take those messy, abstract feelings and pin them down in something real and tangible.

There’s also some evidence to suggest that the pain involved in tattooing can be cathartic, offering a physical release for emotional pain. This could explain why people who self-harm or live with substance misuse or eating disorders might be drawn to the tattoo chair — it’s a place where psychological pain is acknowledged and artistically transformed.

Research suggests there may be correlations between tattoos and mental health.

One 2013 study involving 65 female participants living with anorexia, bulimia, and binge eating disorder explored the relationship between eating disorders, self-injury, and tattoos. Around 51% of the participants reported a history of self-injury, and 27% had at least one tattoo. Those with tattoos were more likely to have a history of self-harm, so the authors suggested that tats could be a form of self-punishment.

However, in an interesting twist, 27% of those with tattoos showed no history of self-injury. These peeps reported more positive body image, higher self-esteem, and fewer mental health struggles.

The relationship between tats and mental health is complex and still being decoded. Further research would help confirm the link between the two.

Tattoos can swing either way on the mental health seesaw. For some folks, getting tattooed is symbolic of their healing process. It says, “Hey, I’ve been through some stuff, but look how I’ve grown!” These tattoos often become symbols of a deeply personal journey, spotlighting moments of triumph over anxiety and depression.

But here’s the flip side: if someone gets inked on a whim or during a rough patch without much thought, that tattoo could be a permanent reminder of a not-so-great time.

In a 2011 study of 82 peeps getting their first tattoo, researchers measured their feelings about their appearance and body both before they got the tattoo and then again immediately and three weeks after the tattooing. The findings showed that right after getting their tattoos, folks of all genders experienced a decrease in appearance anxiety and dissatisfaction. Three weeks later, they reported increased body appreciation, a stronger sense of having a distinctive appearance, heightened feelings of uniqueness, and improved self-esteem. However, female folks experienced increased anxiety related to how others viewed their physique 3 weeks post-tattoo, while males reported a decrease in this type of anxiety.

These results suggest that getting a tattoo can positively affect mental health, but of course, the impact varies among individuals.

Tattoos can be an artistic strategy to enhance your mental health game, but it’s crucial to take a beat and really think it through before you get inked.

Whether you’re looking to mark a milestone, manage the mayhem of anxiety, or remind yourself that everything will be okay, a carefully considered tattoo can be a meaningful addition to your narrative, helping you manage anxiety and positively shaping your story.

So you just got a tattoo — congrats! Time to focus on aftercare. If you want your tattoo to age gracefully, the next few weeks are extra important to…

There are a number of reasons a new or old tattoo can itch. Infections, allergic reactions, and preexisting skin conditions are just a few possible…

#9046. "Intensely physical patterns" cloak Gerhard Richter's self-designed gallery in Doha

Kaleidoscopic patterns adorn the exterior of this pavilion in Doha, Qatar, designed by artist Gerhard Richter with US studio Selldorf Architects as an art gallery.

Simply called Doha Pavilion, the psychedelic structure was conceived a work of both art and architecture for MIA Park – a public space outside the Museum of Islamic Art by IM Pei.

It serves as a permanent pavilion for the site and as a gallery for Richter’s own work.

Richter designed the Doha Pavilion with Selldorf Architects as a reference to his Strip paintings – a series that involved digitally dividing his Abstract Painting artwork into vertical stripes, building on his earlier explorations of colour, pattern and repetition.

“My trip to Doha in 2013 came two years into developing my Strip paintings, and the city’s architecture and history sparked an idea for a pavilion that could unite the thematic threads of that body of work,” said Richter.

“The pavilion’s exterior features decorative tiles based on the patterns that first led me to the Strips,” he continued. “Doha is the right place and the only place for my pavilion.”

Doha Pavilion has a six-sided form, wrapped in psychedelic tiles displaying repeating, kaleidoscopic patterns that recall geometries seen in Islamic art, nodding to the project’s context.

Selldorf Architects founder Annabelle Selldorf said the design reflects a “profound culmination of many years of [Richter’s] research into abstraction”.

“I am grateful for the welcome that Gerhard Richter extended to me, and for the wonderful dialogue that ensued, as my studio made manifest the work that had existed in his mind,” she said.

“This pavilion is the profound culmination of many years of his research into abstraction, with intensely physical patterns that invite you to immerse yourself in their endlessness,” she continued.

“The more I look at them, the more fascinating they become to me as an architectural space to experience.”

Inside, Richter’s paintings and sculptures are displayed throughout the hexagonal gallery space. This includes both archival and new works made especially for the pavilion.

Among the new works is the Strip Tower – a freestanding tripartite sculpture.

The opening of Doha Pavilion coincides with the inaugural edition of Rubaiya Qatar 2026, which is an international visual arts quadrennial.

Elsewhere, Selldorf Architects recently completed the controversial remodel of the National Gallery’s Sainsbury Wing. In an interview with Dezeen after the opening, founder Selldorf said that “what matters is I know why we did things”.

#9045. European Beauty Standards: Impact on Self-Image and Diversity

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.

Keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal. Plus, hear from Siena Liggins, an independent artist and songwriter, about how it affects the music industry and what’s necessary for change.

European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.

“It’s honestly just a trickle effect of something that just exists in our culture on a very wide scale,” Liggins says about European beauty standards.

The Western ideal defines beauty through thinness and whiteness, something American culture was all about for, you know, ever.

But beauty standards often shift in America, moving from one extreme like the rail-thin “heroin chic” look in the 90s to today’s adoration of big butts and busts, with a focus on exercise.

Still, whiteness remains the most represented ideal, and we still obsess over thin bodies, regularly debating which celebrities may or may not be on weight loss medication.

The impression the European beauty standards leave us with is that those who most closely match the call for light skin and eyes, thin noses, etc., are the best or most attractive people — leaving some people of color to internalize the messaging, resulting in feelings of self-hate.

This Western beauty ideal is not only exclusionary — shutting out Black, Indigenous, Arab, and Asian, Pacific Islander people — but it’s also deeply harmful.

The standard is unmistakably splashed across the entertainment and beauty industries, from not finding your makeup shade to not seeing your features represented in media.

It also penetrates our daily work and play, creating societal issues and difficulty with self-esteem that impacts everything from securing and keeping a job to socializing and education, starting as young as nursery school.

For one workplace example, a 2020 study found that white women or Black women with straightened hair are more likely to land job interviews than Black women wearing natural hairstyles like afros, twists, curls, or braids.

Some of the first research on skin color and self-perception among Black children included “the doll test.” Researchers presented Black children, aged 3–7, with four dolls that all looked the same — except for their skin color — and asked them a series of questions about which dolls were nicest or prettiest and which they liked best.

Two-thirds of the Black children chose the white doll. The test was repeated in a similar way in 2005, with 16 of the 21 preschool-aged Black children selecting the white doll.

Needless to say, the beauty standard also negatively impacts the educational system, romantic relationships, and a slew of other dynamics and environments.

“The reality is that you need people to challenge them if you’re ever going to see anything change,” Liggins says about beauty standards.

She points to “AMERICAN REQUIEM,” one song off Beyoncé’s country album Cowboy Carter.

“She talks about how for things to stay the same, they have to change again,” Liggins explains. Though she believes Beyoncé refers to a hope for peace and healing in the United States, Liggins says this concept can lend to beauty standards.

When it comes to the idealistic view that we put on celebrities and pop culture, Liggins says you have to reimagine what it looks like over and over again. “And what that requires is letting in new people, and it can’t just be from a vanity’s perspective,” Liggins says.

Coupled with who is represented in music videos, Liggins says change is also needed at a gatekeeper level. “It has to be the people who are coming up with the ideas and bringing them into fruition who also have to have diversity, not just a thought but of background, culture, and ethnicity,” she says.

Otherwise, Liggins says, we’ll only continue to see spikes in diversity, making inclusion more of a fad than a serious change.

#9042. Should I Exercise with a Phlegmy Cough? What You Need to Know

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

You’re feeling a bit under the weather, but you don’t want to lose the momentum of your fitness routine. So, should you push through and hit the gym, or is it better to rest and let your body heal? Let’s break it down!

Sleep is the best way to help your body recover quickly when you’re sick. But if you’re determined to rise and grind, you could use the “neck check” to decide whether to lace up those sneakers or stay in bed.

Many sports doctors use this theory to say that if your symptoms are above the neck — sniffles, sore throat, or a mild headache — you’re generally good to go for a light workout. But if you’re dealing with chest congestion, a hacking or juicy cough, diarrhea, a fever, or an upset stomach, it’s better to take some time to catch up on your Netflix watchlist.

Big disclaimer: there’s little scientific evidence behind the “neck check,” so use your best judgment.

If you’re going with the above-the-neck rule, exercising with the following symptoms is probably okay.

Going super hard if you have a mild cold is not a good idea. But a light workout, like a walk or a chill Peloton sesh, can be a great way to stay active without overdoing it. Stretching or light yoga might also do the trick.

Stick to light activities like walking for most earaches. Avoid intense workouts like weightlifting, yoga, or pilates, as they can throw off your balance and put pressure on your sinuses, exacerbating the pain.

Light and short workouts are likely fine if your sore throat is mild and lacks fever, cough, or swallowing issues. Remember to stay hydrated — it can ease your sore throat and is beneficial during exercise.

Light activities like brisk walks or gentle bike rides can help for allergy-related stuffy noses. If your nose is blocked, stick to very light activities, focusing on breathing. Skip workouts if you have a fever, chest congestion, or a productive cough with phlegm until you’re symptom-free.

If you’re experiencing the following symptoms, the workout can wait.

Working out with a fever increases dehydration risk and can worsen the fever. Plus, fever saps your muscle strength and coordination, making you more prone to injuries. So, do yourself a favor and skip the workout until you’re back to normal.

An occasional cough is your body’s way of clearing out irritants, but a frequent or phlegmy cough could signal a respiratory infection like a cold, flu, or even pneumonia or asthma. While a tickle-induced cough isn’t a gym deal-breaker, a persistent one is.

Diarrhea and vomiting can dehydrate you, and physical activity only makes that dehydration worse. Feeling weak? That’s a recipe for injury. Plus, stomach bugs are highly contagious. If you feel antsy, stick to light stretching or yoga at home.

The flu hits your respiratory system hard, with symptoms like fever, chills, sore throat, body aches, fatigue, headache, cough, and congestion. If you’ve got the flu, take it easy and give your body some well-earned R&R.

Once symptom-free, ease back into exercise gradually. Start with less intense workouts to avoid overdoing it. As your symptoms fade, you can gradually return to normal activity.

Regular exercise may shorten recovery time, particularly for acute respiratory infections. Listen to your body’s signals to gauge your strength. If you’re still contagious, opt for home or outdoor workouts, so you don’t spread those germs to fellow gym-goers.

P.S. Check in with a healthcare provider if you’re unsure when it’s safe to start exercising again.

#9041. At the Broad, Six Decades of Art Question the Myth of Progress

Two weeks after the 1992 Los Angeles uprising, Los Angeles Times reporter Janny Scott published an essay confronting her own complacency toward the city’s stark inequalities. For years, she’d witnessed the chasm widen between women carrying $3,500 handbags and those wearing trash bags; from her “nice neighborhood where the helicopters don’t come,” she did little to address the disparity. Still, the unrest that followed the acquittal of four LAPD officers charged with beating Rodney King seemed to have broken through the collective apathy. Angelenos, she wrote, were suddenly talking about “things that matter”: race, guilt, poverty, urban policy, to name a few. Despite history offering little reason for optimism, Scott confessed to a sense of hope: “I’m nurturing my first illusion.” Related Articles Christie's Notches a $145.9 M. Sale of 21st-Century Art, Led by a $32.9 M. Basquiat, amid Flagging Energy Piaget's Latest Release Is a Limited-Edition Andy Warhol Camouflage Watch

More than three decades later, artist Guadalupe Rosales found a copy of the newspaper containing Scott’s article on eBay. The headlines “Seeing Ourselves” and “Has the Myth Been Shattered?” registered the same discrepancy she sensed between what she remembered as a child growing up in East LA and how the press perpetuated myths about the city’s seeming collectivity. Rosales was 11 years old in 1992, and she has a distinct memory of her mother rushing the family home from school as smoke stained the usually sun-drenched California sky. As an adult, Rosales has amassed an archive of clippings, photographs, and other ephemera of Chicanx youth culture—much of it crowdsourced through social media—that serves as both a bulwark against that dissonance and a counter to historical erasure and amnesia. “I’m not looking for answers,” she told ARTnews. “But for some kind of physical proof that things really happened, that they’re not just in our memories.”

Rosales’s 2024 sculpture Has the myth been shattered encases that infamous yellowed newspaper in a nearly six-foot-tall aluminum frame fitted with a two-way mirror, illuminated by colorful LED lights. Though it resembles a doorway, the work offers no passage; instead, viewers face their own reflections superimposed over the 1992 text, along with photographs of palm trees and police. The temporal distance between then and now collapses onto a single plane, leaving Scott’s question perpetually suspended in the present.

The work also lends its title to a just-opened exhibition at the Broad in downtown LA. Organized by assistant curator Jen Vanegas Rocha, the presentation brings together works by more than a dozen artists spanning six decades. Recent acquisitions by Rosales and Hank Willis Thomas appear alongside art by Andy Warhol, Barbara Kruger, Glenn Ligon, and Robert Longo, among others. Across prints, paintings, drawings, sculpture, and tapestry, artists appropriate text and images from various forms of public record, drawing attention to the ways media shapes perception of major sociopolitical events. Seen together, the works undermine the assumption that exposing injustice inevitably leads to redress. “There are echoes of the present in the past,” Willis Thomas said. “So is the past present or is the present past?”

The Broad’s founding director, Joanne Heyler, sees that unease as central to the exhibition’s timeliness. “The notion of a linear progression of change unfolding in a dependable, escalating way,” she said, is “becoming harder and harder to believe in.”

Consider the oldest work in the show, Andy Warhol’s Race Riot (1963), in which police dogs attack Black civil-rights demonstrators in Birmingham, Alabama. In 2026, the decades-old image calls to mind the police response to the 2020 protests following the murder of George Floyd, as well as the more recent pro-Palestine and anti-ICE demonstrations nationwide, in which protestors were often battered and tear-gassed. Warhol lifted the photograph directly from a visual essay by Charles Moore in Life magazine, translating the confrontation into a monochromatic silkscreen. Adopting the incendiary rhetoric of contemporary news coverage, he labeled the peaceful demonstrators “rioters.” Race Riot reflects the artist’s own reckoning with the contradictions at the heart of American life: His obsession with celebrities and mass consumption give way to the sensationalized images of death and violence that belie it, like the mangled cars and electric chairs that also feature in his “Death and Disaster” series. Viewers are left to consider whether the relentless circulation of violence sharpens public outrage or gradually dulls our empathy.

For Willis Thomas, Warhol’s Birmingham silkscreen paintings function as “postcards to the future.” By transforming them from documentation to works of art, Warhol has made a case for their continued relevance. Nearby, Willis Thomas’s photo-based Black Survival Guide, or How to Live Through a Police Riot (2018) revisits the same era to recover another history largely omitted from public memory. While researching the aftermath of Martin Luther King Jr.’s assassination, he discovered a typewritten pamphlet offering practical advice to Black residents of Wilmington, Delaware, during the nine-month National Guard occupation in 1968. Onto retroreflective vinyl, Willis Thomas printed excerpts from the pamphlet—advice on how to staunch bleeding or communicate during a power outage, for example—atop archival News Journal photographs of confrontations between armed soldiers and the city’s Black communities. Installed in a darkened gallery, the black-and-white images are invisible until a flash of light illuminates them. Rather than merely encountering the past, the audience actively aids in its recovery. “In some ways the observers become the researchers,” he said.

Histories of state-sanctioned violence and resistance movements similarly converge across a nearly eleven-foot-wide canvas in Mickalene Thomas’s 2021 mixed-media painting The Charnel House (Resist #5). Reworking Picasso’s 1944–45 masterpiece of corpses heaped beneath a table made in response to news footage of liberated Nazi concentration camps, Thomas collages photographs and placards from the Civil Rights and Black Lives Matter movements with the modernist’s fragmented anatomical forms. A poster advertising the Black Panther Party’s free breakfast program appears beside a portrait of Angela Davis and the names of Freddie Gray and Alton Sterling, both killed during encounters with police. Here, grief and trauma are paired with resistance and community building.

The language of dissent assumes a subtler register in Ligon’s Narratives (1993), a suite of nine sepia-toned etchings that mimic the ornate typography and florid prose of 19th-century slave narratives. Ligon replaces accounts of enslavement and escape with details from his early education at a predominantly white private school, his desire for other men, and the circumstances of his career as an artist. In his hands, a literary form that freed Black people used to demonstrate their humanity becomes a medium for contemporary self-portraiture and self-determination.

Museums, of course, too, play a role in shaping public records. Over the past five years, the Broad has acquired work by 26 artists previously unrepresented in its collection, many of whom are of a younger generation and, like Rosales, actively working in LA. Heyler sees these acquisitions as part of an ongoing effort to better reflect the multiplicity of the communities that surround the institution. “We’re not telling one story but many,” she said. “We’re always striving to strengthen the connective tissues between them.”

The exhibition offers an opportunity to showcase many of the newly acquired artists and to extend an art-historical conversation that Heyler traces to exhibitions like “A Forest of Signs: Art in the Crisis of Representation,” a landmark 1989 survey at the Museum of Contemporary Art, just across the street. Bringing together works by 30 American artists, from Jeff Koons to Jenny Holzer, that show examined the unstable boundaries between reality and representation in an increasingly media-saturated society. But the terrain has evolved, Heyler noted. Where artists of that period often exposed the ideologies concealed by authoritative and commercial imagery, audiences today, immersed in social media and generative AI, navigate what she called a “stew of falsehoods and truths.”

Even so, curator Vanegas Rocha hopes her exhibition inspires something more generative than cynicism, in which artists can be seen as the “architects of better futures.” She locates the potential for systemic change in the power of an individual aesthetic encounter. “It can teach you about the world, about others, about yourself,” she said. “That single moment can have a ripple effect, leading to a collective difference.” Rosales, likewise, hasn’t relinquished hope. Citing José Esteban Muñoz’s 2009 queer theory book Cruising Utopia, she described hope as an ever-receding horizon that we must continue to endeavor toward. “We are a people that don’t give up,” she said, noting that her mother also took her to protests from an early age. “Standing up for each other, even when you don’t see it right away, does pay off.” Progress, she suggests, may not be linear or inevitable, but that doesn’t make it an illusion. In her mirror, the unresolved question—“Has the Myth Been Shattered?”—is cast back onto the people who might yet determine the answer.
